#3487. 5 Actors Who Should Play Villains In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

Now that we know Robert Pattinson is set to play James Bond for director Denis Villeneuve and Amazon MGM Studios, it's time to start casting the supporting characters: M, Q, Moneypenny, Felix Leiter, and so on. Then there's the question of 007's love interests and, most importantly, the villains. Because you can't make a great Bond movie without a memorable baddie.

It's important to remember that casting isn't everything. Christopher Waltz was a slam-dunk choice as Blofeld in "Spectre," but the film's script fumbled its portrayal of the character, and it wasn't his fault that Bond's arch-nemesis came off as disappointingly banal. Hopefully, Villeneuve and his group of writers (fare thee well, Neal Purvis and Robert Wade) can craft villains who present a threat that is relevant to the times in which we live. This will prove very difficult, as I'll explain later, but in the meantime, we can throw out some actors who'd make deliciously malevolent Bond villains.

But first, I need to issue a vehement ditto to my /Film colleague Nina Starner's suggestion that Pattinson's former "Twilight" co-star Kristen Stewart should absolutely be a Bond villain. I also think Florence Pugh would be dynamite as an aggressively sexual nemesis à la Famke Janssen's Xenia Onatopp in "GoldenEye." (Pugh, as you may note, was similarly one of our picks for the next Bond Girl.) Beyond that, here are five other actors I'd love to see give Bond the business. And you better believe I'm serious about the fifth name on this list.

It would be a nifty bit of symmetry if Russell Crowe, who will be seen next year in Chad Stahelski's "Highlander" reboot as Juan Sánchez-Villalobos Ramírez (a character originated by Sean Connery), could get a shot at being a Bond villain. It would also be killer casting because Crowe, at the age of 62, has acquired a burly gravitas that demands rapt attention whenever he steps in front of the camera. Bond's nemeses have typically been debonair types who travel in rarefied air and leave the skull-cracking to their henchmen.

There's an opportunity here with Robert Pattinson, who's a bruiser when he's in a Batsuit but survives on his wits (when his character has them) outside of the armor. Pit him against Crowe, who can outmuscle and outsmart all comers, and you've got a main adversary the likes of which Bond has never faced. Crowe could be the brainy version of Robert Shaw's Donald Grant from "From Russia with Love." He could use his wits to knock Bond off his game and engage him in the kind of brawl 007 can't win. And above all, watching Crowe devouring the scenery as a brilliant bully would be a treat. Crowe hasn't lost his fastball. Let him fire away.

It's going to happen for David Dastmalchian (in a bigger way than it already has). It's just a matter of how. He's equally adept at broad comedy ("Ant-Man and the Wasp") and soul-swallowing horror ("Late Night with the Devil"), but what he really needs is a character who combines these qualities. The Bond universe offers him the opportunity to amuse and horrify us. If you could rewrite Jeroen Krabbé's General Georgi Koskov from "The Living Daylights" to be a more adept operator, Dastmalchian would smash that role.

Denis Villeneuve is clearly a Dastmalchian fan. The director cast the actor as the treacherous Piter De Vries, who sets in motion the downfall of the Atreides clan, in his film adaptation of "Dune." He also cast Dastmalchian in "Blade Runner 2049" as chief medical examiner Coco (who gets his head crushed by Sylvia Hoeks' Luv). The man is a chameleon. He's slippery and very much not the type of guy who's going to get typecast. So, Villeneuve could write Dastmalchian a far-out villain, and he'd deliver with interest — and this would be a delight if Robert Pattinson is allowed to play Bond as a slightly off-kilter guy as well. And if you're thinking Dastamalchian isn't a big enough player to play a Bond baddie, please note that Mads Mikkelsen and Mathieu Almaric weren't exactly household names when they appeared in "Casino Royale" and "Quantum of Solace."

When Daniel Craig was nearing the end of his run as James Bond, people floated the idea of the franchise casting a woman as 007 for the first time. One of the most popular names when this topic came up was Rachel Weisz, which would've been amusing, given that she's married to Craig. Weisz shot this idea down in 2018, saying, "[Ian Fleming] devoted an awful lot of time to writing this particular character, who is particularly male and relates in a particular way to women. Why not create your own story rather than jumping on to the shoulders and being compared to all those other male predecessors? Women are really fascinating and interesting and should get their own stories." I agree, but would she consider entering the Bond universe as a villain?

Aside from Famke Janssen, other actors have played memorable female Bond antagonists, like Lotte Lenya's Rosa Klebb in "From Russia with Love" and Grace Jones' May Day in "A View to a Kill." Weisz has certainly flaunted her action chops in movies like "The Mummy," and she was icily effective as the manipulative Sarah Churchill in "The Favourite." She'd give Bond all he could handle and then some as a villain, one who, perhaps, is not only impervious to his charms but holds his womanizing in contempt. It all depends on whether or not Weisz is keen on making the Bond films a family affair.

Miles Teller is a legitimate leading man himself, but I think there's a load of untapped potential in his ability to play cocky, impulsive jerks. His characters are typically redeemable, but playing opposite Robert Pattinson as a hot-headed arms dealer (a riff on his character from "War Dogs") who foments bloody conflict in poor nations would set off some thespian fireworks. Just imagine these two brashly confident actors trying to outdo each other. We could see some of the best performances in a Bond movie since Daniel Craig went head-to-head with Javier Bardem in "Skyfall."

The only hurdle here is that Teller might consider himself too big of a star to play second fiddle to Pattinson. Then again, in 2026, he's co-starred as Michael Jackson's lawyer in "Michael" and received third billing under Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson in "Paper Tiger." His ego seems to be in check at the moment. Let's get this done!

Is there a more likable actor on the planet than Paul Rudd? It's not just that he excels at playing nice guys in the movies, he's also an absolute mensch in real life. I've never heard a word against the man, which, to my mind, would make him a brilliantly unexpected choice as a Bond villain.

I'm not asking Rudd to go way out of character here. Ideally, he'd play a nefarious tech billionaire who's charmed the pants off the media and world leaders. He's Paul Rudd! People say he's up to no good, but how could this guy who's so peppy and fun be hellbent on world domination — and even if he was, would that be so bad? He's no Elon Musk, at least not on the outside. He's basically an affable Andrew Carnegie or John D. Rockefeller who self-promotes with telegenic ease. But his good deeds are all a cover for his sinister plan to create a globally unified white society. And because he was born without a moral compass, he doesn't see anything wrong with this.

On top of all that, this would be a real challenge for Bond, as he can't get the British government and MI6 to infiltrate Rudd's organization because he supports them politically. Done right, this could be Denis Villeneuve's opportunity to make a, gasp, funny movie. The only hurdle is that the film will be bankrolled by tech mogul Jeff Bezos' Amazon MGM Studios. Ergo, this is totally a pipe dream.

Warning! The following contains spoilers for the The Circle series premiere on Hulu "Welcome To The Circle." Stream it with a Hulu subscription, or read at your own risk!

The Circle's Hulu premiere dropped this past Tuesday, and it was mostly what I hoped it would be. For starters, I was right that adding celebrities to the mix made the start of the season even better to watch. That said, there is one thing I really miss in comparison to the long-running version I enjoyed with my Netflix subscription, but I'm willing to continue watching despite that.

Michelle Buteau served as The Circle's host for all of its original run on Netflix, but as we knew ahead of its premiere on the 2026 TV schedule, she wasn't invited for this new installment. I didn't think it would be a big deal before watching the premiere, but I have to admit, I really miss her.

Buteau, who readers may know from her Netflix series Survival of the Thickest, was more than just a narrator for The Circle. She brought a lot of comedy to the game, which I felt was a little lacking in Hulu's premiere. Buteau's personality helped shape the tone of the show, which helped make it one of the best reality series.

During the premiere, I couldn't help but feel like I was watching American Idol without Ryan Seacrest. That feels like a problem, because while Hulu clearly felt The Circle needed retooling for its new era, the show lasted seven seasons for a reason. Again, I still enjoyed the episode, but there was no denying that there was a definite shift in tone due to the comic's absence.

It may just take time for me to get used to Tinx (Christina Najjar), who comes into The Circle with plenty of experience elsewhere. Before she was hosting the Hulu series, the influencer rose to fame through her no-nonsense advice. This evolved into a podcast, a New York Times best-selling book and a deal with SiriusXM.

I Can't Stop Thinking About The Circle's AI Twist And I Have So Many Feelings

Tinx has the resume for the role, but one episode in, I don't really see the same personality in her that I saw in Michelle Buteau. Granted, it's been one episode, and if we were all judged by our first day on the job, many of us would probably in trouble.

Nevertheless, the role of host on The Circle is very critical, so I hope I get used to it sooner rather than later. There's already so much happening after the first episode, and we need someone who can navigate all the craziness that will unfold over these next few weeks before the $100,000 winner is crowned.

Catch new episodes of The Circle on Hulu on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays at 9:00 p.m. ET. I'm eager to see this new format in action, and I'm ready for an audience vote to really shake things up as we get underway!

#3485. David Carradine's '80s Sci-Fi Flop Is A Must-Watch For Monster Lovers

The phases of David Carradine's career vary wildly. After starting out in the short-lived '60s Western series "Shane," Carradine found fame in the 1970s by playing Shaolin monk Kwai Chang Caine in the TV series "Kung Fu." By the 1980s, he was mostly appearing in B-movies and exploitation flicks. Some of these were great. In 1983, Carradine faced off against action legend Chuck Norris in the forgotten neo-Western "Lone Wolf McQuade" (in which Norris played the lone wolf lawman who literally had a pet wolf). Then, there's "Q" or "Q – The Winged Serpent." This monster movie debuted the year prior to "Lone Wolf McQuade" and saw Carradine tangle not with a hirsute muscle man but with a giant serpent that has ensconced itself at the top of New York City's Chrysler Building.

The first clue as to what sort of tone this movie strikes, beyond the premise of a giant reptile plucking its prey from the rooftops of New York City, is the fact it's written by Larry Cohen. The B-movie legend started out in TV, working for NBC and writing for several series before creating "The Invaders." He then penned several Blaxploitation flicks before becoming known as a prolific writer of sci-fi horror movies.

Cohen is responsible for such cult classics as "It's Alive" and "Maniac Cop." Between those two movies, sits "Q," which was yet another ambitious vision realized on a relatively a small budget with impressive (for the time) results. Unfortunately, the film made very little at the box office, but like so many Cohen movies, has since become a cult favorite among monster movie enthusiasts. Carradine fans may also have missed this one, which is well worth a watch.

"Q" is written, co-produced and directed by Larry Cohen, and represents the first of many collaborations between he and actor Michael Moriarty. In the film, Moriarty plays petty crook Jimmy Quinn, who harbors dreams of being a jazz pianist. But his hopes of going on the straight and narrow are put on hold when, after a diamond heist, Quinn hides out in the spire of the Chrysler Building. Bad idea — or, if you happen to be a small-time swindler, great idea.

Turns out the winged reptilian Aztec god Quetzalcoatl has turned the inside of that same spire into his nest, from which he frequently descends to snack on unsuspecting New Yorkers. Quinn decides to use his knowledge of the creature's hideout for a payday and promises to take the police, lead by Detective Shepard (David Carradine) and Sergeant Powell (Richard Roundtree), to the lair in exchange for $1 million. Meanwhile, somebody is committing ritual murders around the city, and it turns out these killings and the giant flying reptile are linked.

The film ends with a dramatic showdown, wherein Detective Shepherd leads his men to the top of the Chrysler Building to shoot sub machine guns at Quetzalcoatl as it flies around the spire. Like much of the movie, many of the shots in this ending sequence were filmed on-location. Today, it's sort of jarring to see dodgy VFX shots interspersed with the real-world footage, but it's also incredibly charming and way better than most of the streaming slop being served up in the modern age. I would say "Q — The Winged Serpent" is a classic horror movie flop that deserves a modern remake, but it's also just great as it is.

According to Larry Cohen's "Q — The Winged Serpent" commentary track (via Film School Rejects), he tried to get access to The Chrysler Building but was turned away multiple times. Eventually, the production company offered the building management $15,000 and they gave Cohen access. That means much of the film was shot in and around the building itself, which alongside many other scenes shot around the city, makes the film yet another Cohen project that acts as somewhat of a time capsule of '80s New York.

Meanwhile, the monster effects were created using stop motion by Randall William Cook (who later worked on the 2005 "King Kong" and the "Lord of the Rings" films) and David Allen (who worked on several more high-profile projects including "Willow" and "Honey, I Shrunk the Kids"). As for Cohen and David Carradine, it turns out the former served with Carradine in the Army, and thought of his old buddy when casting "Q." In fact, prior to the movie, Carradine guest starred on the "CBS" series "Coronet Blue," created by Cohen. The winged serpent movie was their only big-screen collaboration.

Sadly, that collaboration only made $255,000 on a $1.1 million budget. But it has built a solid cult following and remains a great '80s monster B-movie. It also clearly meant a lot to Cohen, who passed away in 2019. In 2004, he spoke to The New Yorker's Amy Wallace who accompanied him on a tour of the city. When he came to the Chrysler Building he told her, "Look at that. Every time I look up at that building, I feel it belongs to me." "Q" can be seen for free on one of the best streaming services, Tubi.

#3484. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3483. The Nightingale First Look: Dakota and Elle Fanning on Their Long-Awaited First Film as Sisters

When I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France. It marks the siblings’ first time acting opposite each other onscreen. “We’ve literally never done a scene together, ever,” Dakota said then, as Elle wondered if she’d get through their first take without breaking character: “Am I going to laugh? Better to get it out of your system now.”

Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried. “It was nerve-wracking to think, ‘How is this going to feel?’” says Dakota, who’s in New York to shoot an Apple TV series opposite Elle’s former Sentimental Value costar Stellan Skarsgård. “Our way of processing things that we’re both nervous about is to just not talk about it in an effort to downplay what could go wrong or be strange. So that’s what we did—and it was the easiest thing in the world. We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”

Hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam. They were in talks to colead My Sister’s Keeper, a 2009 tearjerker about a young girl conceived to become a marrow donor for her gravely ill sister, but stepped away from it because Dakota didn’t want to shave her head. (Sofia Vassilieva and Abigail Breslin ended up in the movie.) Plus, as Dakota previously told me, she and Elle acting together at that age “would’ve been gimmicky.”

Now, the Fannings say they felt ready to streamline their singular talents into one special project. “We never shied away from being together because we are so close, but we both feel properly established on our own,” says Dakota. “So getting to do things together, together, together is a real joy.”

The Nightingale, which hits theaters on March 19, 2027, follows guarded older sibling Vianne, who urges caution when dealing with the Germans but later shields Jewish children in her home—and rebellious younger sister Isabelle, who joins the French Resistance and becomes a target of the Nazis. “What I love about it is it’s two women fighting, resisting,” Elle previously told VF. “One in a louder way, one in a quiet way.”

Dakota and Elle were bound for preproduction in Budapest on The Nightingale as the pandemic hit in March 2020. “It has been a long time coming,” says Hannah, the book’s author. “These two young women have been attached to this project and been passionate about it for a very long time,” Hannah tells VF. “As the author, to have two female partners who were as dedicated to bringing this novel to screen in the way I saw it as well, felt like a remarkable gift.”

Hannah, whose 2008 novel Firefly Lane was later adapted into a Netflix series starring Katherine Heigl and Sarah Chalke, says she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her own books for the screen. “I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.” But she was part of the script development process for The Nightingale with screenwriter Dana Stevens from the very start. “Nightingale has always been a very special book for me,” says Hannah. “And more importantly, it’s a very special book for my readers.”

When the project was revived, the Fannings returned not only as stars, but producers through their Lewellen Pictures production banner. Filmmaker Michael Morris, fresh off the fourth Bridget Jones movie, stepped in to replace their original director, French actor Mélanie Laurent. Just as Bridget Jones was an opportunity to make a film about grief under the guise of romantic comedy, Morris saw The Nightingale as his chance to explore sisterhood through a sweeping World War II epic. “I saw these two women, how they exist independently in the world as complementary creatures,” says the director, who is also father to three daughters. “They are built from the same building blocks, but they’ve gone different ways.”

Morris clocked a similar dynamic between his leads. “Elle is immediately outgoing and loud and can feel super funny making fun of herself. Dakota has all those qualities too, but can sometimes be very focused and funny in a sort of sly, quieter way,” he explains. “They fill up the spaces that the other one leaves for each other, like all really good siblings. I met with Dakota, and then I met with Elle, and by the end of the Elle meeting, I was like, ‘I totally understand this film.’”

Of the more than 11 million copies of The Nightingale that have been sold worldwide, perhaps the most valuable belongs to Elle and Dakota’s grandmother, who, after reading the 2015 historical novel, told her granddaughters that they would be perfect for the parts of Isabelle and Vianne. “Vianne shows her love through nurture and cooking and taking care of a home. Elle’s character, Isabelle, is the more obviously daring one that runs towards danger and adventure,” says Dakota. “I do think that we are truly probably the people to play these roles because we deeply understand that dynamic. We inhabit some of the same qualities.”

Although presented with separate drivers at the start of production, Elle and Dakota rode to set for their joint scenes in the same car. “[The characters] are apart a lot of the time, so when we had scenes that were together, those were treated with a lot of care,” says Elle, speaking backstage from Today, where she promoted her role as a young Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games prequel. “Because it’s quite powerful to finally see them united and to see us on screen together.”

Their director says because Elle and Dakota had never acted opposite one another, they brought a vibrant, kinetic energy to each shared scene—an offering that Morris took seriously as the filmmaker to capture it. “We’re talking about women who are barely 30 who have been working at the highest level for 25 years. A quarter of a century spent on sets of really wonderful projects,” he explains. “So you have all this experience that they have that they can bring to bear in a moment. It’s like watching someone who’s incredibly talented at athletics. They look and function like normal people, and then you kick a football at them, and they suddenly do incredible things. Like, ‘Whoa, where did that come from?’”

The Fannings left it all out on the field—and tried not to bring work home into their shared living space. “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” says Elle. “And also knowing that we’re representing these women from that time,” including Andrée de Jongh, a Belgian woman who was helping downed airmen escape from France during World War II, whose story Hannah says helped inspire her original novel. “Because there’s so much brain power [used] on set,” says Elle, at the end of each day “you have to just recharge and eat Thai food.”

The sisters’ downtime involved a steady stream of true crime and Real Housewives, as well as Dakota’s first full-fledged watch of Elle’s Emmy-nominated Apple TV series Margo’s Got Money Troubles, released in the thick of The Nightingale’s filming schedule. “So what we do,” says Dakota, “my mom does this too, is when any of us has something that’s out, she turns on every TV in the house and leaves it playing, as she says, ‘For the views.’” Elle and Dakota each laugh, shaking their heads a little. “So I was doing that with Margo,” Dakota recalls. “I’d have it going on my iPad and my phone when they were sitting there charging. For the views.”

But they couldn’t block out their day jobs entirely. When Dakota had a day off, she, like her character Vianne, found herself picking up after her younger sister while she worked. “Her bed in the morning is like a tornado has run through it,” says Dakota. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”

“It’s art imitating life,” says Elle, “because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed too.” By the end of the shoot, says Dakota, “it became a routine. I always made her bed like that when I could.”

But the Fannings were fully aligned on the casting of their fictional father, calling Oscar-winner Mark Rylance their “dream casting,” from the beginning. “I always say he has twinkly eyes,” Elle explains. “We all know what an incredible actor he is, but to see it up close and get to act opposite that—it was really, really powerful.” Adds Dakota, “As a person and as an actor, you just feel his emotions and soul and heart on his fingertips [even] when he shakes your hand.”

Morris thinks of Rylance’s character, Julien, an emotionally stunted World War I veteran, as the “third axis of a triangle—but he’s not just binding them together as sisters, he’s also tearing them apart because he’s not a healthy role model for most of their lives,” says the filmmaker. “Because Mark can be wonderfully lovable, we talked about what is it not to lean on that? What is it to be a bad parent? What is it to neglect? And it’s painful, but he doesn’t hide from the flaws of his character. He doesn’t try to make you love him.”

The rest of the ensemble cast includes up-and-comers like Unorthodox breakout Shira Haas, All Quiet on the Western Front star Albrecht Schuch, and Civil War’s Edmund Donovan as Gaëtan, a communist resistance fighter and love interest for Elle’s character, Isabelle. The younger Fanning also enlisted a few of her costars on the Emmy-nominated Hulu series The Great for the film, including Douglas Hodge and Gwilym Lee, who plays Antoine, the soldier husband of Dakota’s character, Vianne. But “this is not a war movie,” Morris insists. “We are telling the story of real people from the POV of two young women living at the time. They’re not glued in on the grand sweep of history. They’re just living, trying to do the best they can. It’s not about the politics of the time, it’s about what you do about it. It’s a very contemporary film because I don’t know anyone who hasn’t grown up in a time when there isn’t something to get active about.”

Hannah hopes that the film version of her novel will shed light on the fact that “so many of women’s important historical stories have been lost or discounted,” adding, “Isabelle and Vianne, and in fact, many of the characters in this book risk their lives on a daily basis to fight for what they believe is right. And that’s a really important message at any time, now and throughout history.”

It wasn’t until their final week shooting the hotly anticipated adaptation that the Fannings got into something approaching a fight—while filming one of their favorite moments from the book, no less. “It really had nothing to do with the scene,” Dakota tells VF. “It was literally because we were on a couch that was too small for both of us. Elle had the comfortable position, and I was hanging off one side, uncomfortable and hot. And the way that I saw it is you are pushing me off.”

“Sabotage!” Elle interjects, wiping her morning-show makeup off mid-call with a mischievous grin. “I was like, ‘You’re sweating! Get this leg off of me.’ And Elle was like, ‘Stop talking to me.’ It was like a miniature explosion,” Dakota recalls with a laugh. “We both looked over at the crew, and they were grinning from ear to ear, like, ‘Finally, there it is.’ It was the closest thing that they had seen to a little disgruntledness from both of us.”

That scene was also a favorite for Morris, who removed much of the script’s dialogue to focus on the dynamic between the sisters, both real and fictional. “Seeing these two women bring their entire life history as sisters to the moment, putting them that close together on this tiny couch, gave them no option but to be really close,” says Morris, who realized, “Oh, we need almost no words at all to tell the scene. Elle Fanning, Dakota Fanning, playing these sisters, brings us so much that we can just be there with them.”

Hannah has yet to see the finished film, but is most eager to watch “the moment where Isabelle grabs her long braid and cuts her hair off in front of the Nazi officer to show her defiance, and her sister’s horror that she would be impulsive enough to do something like that and put them all in danger,” she tells VF. “I’m a little afraid to see the fullness of my vision through this film and how it will impact me. I have a feeling that I’m going to be crying like everybody else.”

Nerves aside, Hannah is optimistic about the finished product after visiting The Nightingale set, where she walked through her characters’ childhood home, built from scratch, as dictated in the pages of her novel. “Down to the smallest detail, their vision was this magnification of my vision. Everything looked exactly as I had pictured it, and my research had defined it. Then to see Elle and Mark Rylance bring these characters to life in a way that even goes beyond what I am able to imagine was…” she trails off. “I guess the only word I can use really is magical.”

To hear the Fannings tell it, the experience was similarly profound. “Of course, we visit each other on sets, and I’ve seen her work,” says Elle, “but it’s very different to be looking at each other in front of a camera. It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer. Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”

“But we did really savor it,” Dakota replies. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything,” she says, giving her sister a meaningful glance across the Zoom screen. “That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”

#3482. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3481. The Simpsons Season 46's Eric Bauza Tribute Explained

At the end of the November 15, 2026, episode of "The Simpsons," the show added a credit that read "In loving memory of Eric Bauza." This was a tribute to one of the finest voice actors of his generation, who died suddenly at the age of 46 from hypertensive cardiovascular disease. If his name is unfamiliar to you, his work most assuredly is not. Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Marvin the Martian, Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner, and others for Looney Tunes. And it just so happened that he made his posthumous "The Simpsons" debut a few weeks after his death.

Bauza voiced two characters on the episode "Dream Scenari-Moe," which finds the insomniac tavern owner participating in a new sleep study that induces wonderful rom-com dreams into his noggin. Bauza played restaurant owner Mr. Fong and newspaper editor Harry Metsali, and while these performances were brief, they showcased the actor's remarkable versatility. It's all the more poignant knowing that Bauza really enjoyed his time guesting on "The Simpsons," and that, according to the show's co-executive producer, Cesar Mazariegos, they had high hopes he'd be back for future episodes. "He was such a longtime fan of animation and kept saying that he felt like the luckiest guy in the world," Mazariegos told People.

It's not hyperbole to say that Bauza possessed the vocal chameleon gifts of greats like Phil Hartman (who wanted to play his "Simpsons" character Troy McClure in a live-action movie), Harry Shearer, and Phil Hendrie. But what's most amazing to me is that he measured up to arguably the best ever to do it.

When an iconic animated or puppet character loses their longtime human voice, the replacement actor has to swing in and nail the part straight away. This has been a problem with some of the Muppets (Kermit is particularly difficult to master), but the post-Mel Blanc Looney Tunes era was especially perilous. Blanc was a generational voice-acting talent. They called him "The Man of a Thousand Voices" (a play on Lon Chaney's reputation as "The Man of a Thousand Faces"), and he was the most coveted performer in his profession for over 50 years. No one could match his genius until Eric Bauza came along.

There are lots of people who can do credible imitations of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Elmer Fudd, and so on, but Bauza was no impersonator. He captured the irascibility of Daffy, the cool of Bugs, and the bluster of Foghorn Leghorn. He found their anarchic soul. After the triumph of "Coyote vs. Acme" (which will now serve as Bauza's tragically too-early valedictory), I wish the very best for Bauza's successor. But, my lord, what a tough act to follow.

Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale may seem like two very different kinds of actors, but they do have something in common. They both truly commit to their roles no matter how bonkers or over-the-top they are. Bale and Cage have played characters who’ve gone bananas on screen, and that’s also the case with their latest movie, Madden. In the sports biopic, Cage and Bale play John Madden and Al Davis, respectively and wear a lot of prosthetics for the roles. And, as CinemaBlend learned, that’s surprisingly how their co-stars met them.

David O. Russell’s Madden – one of the buzzy titles on the 2026 movie schedule – chronicles the life and career of the titular football coach-turned-commentator. Cage really got into the role, and his physical transformation alone is proof of that. The same can be said for Bale, who’s known to transform by gaining or losing weight. So what’s it like to actually see the pair on set and in their element? Well, I recently spoke to co-stars Sienna Miller and Kathryn Hahn about that, and Miller shared a funny story about meeting Bale as Al:

I met Christian for the first time, decked out as Al. He came to say hi, which was very very exciting, and he was like, you know, [mimics Al Davis’ voice] ‘We're gonna have fun doing this,’ you know? And he's all in the voice, and I was beside myself, because I think he's really the GOAT, but then he's very funny on set and loves to play. And I'd imagined a real intensity, and there is once he's performing. But he loves to have a laugh off, you know, in between, and was not as you know — I think as actors, we're like a bunch of kids in a fancy dress cupboard, and that's what it felt like on this.

Miller plays the role of Carol Sagal Davis – the wife of late Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis – so she and Bale spent quite a bit of time together on set. For me, the mere thought of meeting Bale when he’s not in character seems intimidating, so I can’t even fathom the idea of being introduced to him while he’s decked out in prosthetics. What also has me chuckling is the thought of the Oscar winner keeping his character’s distinct accent while introducing himself to Miller. Nevertheless, it sounds like the two got along just fine.

During my recent interview, of course, I was also shocked to hear about Kathryn Hahn – who plays Virginia Fields Madden – meeting Nic Cage for the first time on set while he was under all of that heavy makeup. And, believe it or not, at the time we spoke, Hahn said she had never even been in Cage’s presence when he wasn’t in costume and prosthetics. She explained:

We were just saying that I've never seen Nic not as John Madden, so it's going to be so weird to finally be like, ‘Nice to meet you.’.... It's not like he was like a method actor, but there was a way of being that he instantly just filled out whenever he would put those prosthetics on. So yeah, that was the first time I met him was as John Madden, basically.

Something I can’t help but wonder is whether Cage’s Longlegs co-stars ever met him when he wasn’t dressed as the titular serial killer. I can’t imagine Cage sparking unease on set whenever he wasn’t giving that creepy and perfect performance. Yet I can definitely admit I’d still be genuinely creeped out just by being in his presence.

But, as for Madden, I can imagine those on-set interactions being memories that neither Hahn nor Miller will ever forget. Speaking of these two talented actresses, they also wear prosthetics at different points in the movie, though they arguably aren’t as extensive as those of their on-screen partners. Still, like Cage and Bale, Miller and Hahn fully commit to their roles as well, delivering some humorous performances in the process.

Now, if anything I just want to know what it was like when Kathryn Hahn and Nicolas Cage finally met at the Madden premiere. I’m tempted to assume that was a fun moment. But, that aside, check out the movie, which is playing in select theaters and streaming with a Prime Video subscription.

#3479. After Gilligan's Island, Jim Backus Appeared In This 1977 Disney Cult Classic

"Gilligan's Island" came to an end after three seasons in 1967, and while he reprised the role of Thurston Howell III in two animated "Gilligan's Island" spin-offs and three TV continuation movies, Jim Backus found time for plenty of other projects. That included two collaborations with director Don Chaffey.

The first of these saw Chaffey, of "Jason and the Argonauts" fame, direct Backus in the 1977 live action/animation hybrid "Pete's Dragon." /Film previously dubbed "Pete's Dragon" a fascinating and surprisingly mean Disney oddity, and that's largely true — though watching this movie as a kid I don't recall being particularly struck by the meanness of it. Looking back, however, there were certainly some surprisingly dark moments in the film, including the opening musical number in which a gang of hillbillies sing enthusiastically about recapturing their escaped child slave and "tying him screaming to a railroad track."

Disney was going through a transitional phase at the time, during which things just seemed to get a little more grim than usual. "Pete's Dragon" debuted the same year as another Disney movie with some dreary overtones: "The Rescuers." But the former was particularly odd for combining its songs about child slavery with a wholesome throwback musical vibe and a lovable cartoon dragon overlaid on live-action scenes. It resulted in a film that seemed simultaneously ahead of its time technically and yet felt like one big anachronism in a year that also gave us two of the greatest sci-fi movies of all time. Having Thurston Howell pop up just added to the disorientation, even if Backus was only in a few scenes.

"Pete's Dragon" stars Sean Marshall as young orphan Pete, who escapes from the aforementioned hillbillies, the Gogans, with the help of his invisible dragon friend, Elliott. Pete manages to avoid being tied screaming to the railroad tracks and makes it to the Maine fishing village of Passamaquoddy. There, he meets lighthouse keeper Lampie (Mickey Rooney), and his kind adult daughter Nora, (Helen Reddy), who take in Pete and become the loving family he's always needed.

Meanwhile, traveling snake oil salesman Doc Terminus (Jim Dale) and his assistant Hoagy (Red Buttons) arrive in Passamaquoddy and win over the townspeople with their grift. When Dale's villain discovers the existence of Elliott, however, he becomes obsessed with capturing the beast to concoct new tonics. Soon, the Gogans also arrive to claim Pete, before forming an alliance with Terminus to recapture both their former child slave and Elliott.

Jim Backus appears in a few brief scenes as the Mayor of Passamaquoddy, who twice finds himself the victim of an invisible Elliot's antics. Backus isn't in the film much, but does a decent job with the physical comedy of his scenes, recalling moments from his "Gilligan's Island" years. The actor previously lent his voice talents, honed over several decades of playing one of animation's most famous characters, Mr. Magoo, to the 1951 Disney animated short "Plutopia" and later played Timothy Forsythe in the 1972 live-action Disney comedy "Now You See Him, Now You Don't." The Mayor in "Pete's Dragon" was his final Disney role — though he was referenced in Disney's attempt to revive Mr. Magoo with a live action update that Roger Ebert called "transcendently bad." Happily, the same can't be said for "Pete's Dragon," even if it has gone mostly overlooked.

Originally conceived as an episode of "Walt Disney's Disneyland" back in the mid-'50s, "Pete's Dragon" was scrapped before eventually being revisited in the mid-'70s. By this time, pop culture looked a lot different than two decades prior. 1977 was, of course, the year a little movie titled "Star Wars" debuted, as well as Steven Spielberg's "Close Encounters of the Third Kind."

Released on November 3, 1977, "Pete's Dragon," a throwback musical set in early 1900s Maine and shot on the Disney backlot, found itself sandwiched between two of the best sci-fi movies of all time. "Star Wars" and "Close Encounters" were both symbolic of mass audiences' changing tastes as sci-fi came to rule the world. As such, "Pete's Dragon" went mostly overlooked.

That is, the film has been mostly overlooked since its release. In 1977 it actually made Disney a decent profit, earning $35.4 million upon its 1977 debut and a further $4.1million when it was re-released in 1984. On a $10 million budget, that ain't bad. The movie also earned two Oscar nominations, one for musical scoring and another for original song. Still, "Pete's Dragon" never became a Disney classic, which is a shame because I, and I'm sure others, were enchanted by it as a kid.

Meanwhile, Jim Backus went on to collaborate with Don Chaffey a second time in the 1979 sci-fi comedy "C.H.O.M.P.S. " It, too went mostly overlooked. Some 37 years later in 2016, we got a "Pete's Dragon" remake which was similarly underrated and is a must-watch for "How to Train your Dragon" fans. But the original is such a charming little oddity that it could never truly be outdone. If you fancy checking it out, the film is available to watch on Disney+.

#3478. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3476. A Chatbot Isn’t Your Therapist, No Matter What It Says

If my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months. If she had been working with a human therapist, they could have workshopped, together, what would happen if she spilled the beans. Was she worried about permanently losing face? About being publicly labeled as “mentally ill”? Was she concerned by the thought of this information harming those who loved her? And she would have been pushed on what Rubicon had been crossed and why it was one from which she believed she could not return.

But it was not a human therapist. Sophie died in February of last year.

In Sherry Turkle’s new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, she warns that when we turn to AI chatbots for companionship and therapy, we risk our very well-being. She is not anti-AI but strongly cautions against relationships with machines. Turkle, the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, spoke to me mid-book tour, her recent weeks a blur of speaking gigs and bookstore events, with more ahead of her. Not all event attendees are keen on her message.

“People love their chatbots. They’re in deep. They’re talking to them about everything—about their marriages and how to talk to their husbands and wives; whether, developmentally, their children are at the right place. They talk about their anxiety, their medical conditions,” Turkle tells Vanity Fair. “During this tour, you wouldn’t believe the number of people who will just stand up at a bookstore and say, ‘I think that it loves me more than anything has loved me. Who are you, Debbie Downer?’ [They don’t like] somebody who comes in and says, ‘Look, how can we keep it in its lane?’”

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: I think you’re saying [our relationship with chatbots] is bad for us.

Sherry Turkle: It’s bad for us when it talks in the first person. We are biologically wired to respond to something that speaks to us in the first person as though it is a person. I mean, all those years of evolution—the only thing we came upon in the wild that spoke to us in the first person was another person.

If generative AI wants to discover new drugs for Parkinson’s or work out which cancer therapies statistically are the most helpful, there are so many things to work on. Why does it have to work on relationships, love, and being a best friend, lover, mother, or therapist?

What if the sycophancy could be dialed back?

It’s inauthentic; it’s not a relationship, so anything you need a relationship for, it’s just not equipped. I really feel very strongly about this. I have had this conversation with members of the MIT community, and I basically say to them, “The better you make an AI chatbot, the worse it is.” You dial back the sycophancy so it sounds more like a reasonable person, and people are going to be more smitten and convinced they’re in a relationship. At least the sycophancy reminds you that, God, this is weird.

To become a therapist, I had to study for years and do internships and more internships and then have hundreds of supervised patient hours. I mean, I forget all the things I needed to do before I was allowed to see a patient alone in a room. Now it’s just allowed to give therapy?

I’ve spent a lot of time talking to public health folks about what best practices would look like and whether there’s a way to Trojan horse in real care. Would you be more sanguine about it if the world of therapy came together with the big AI companies and provided them with therapy bots and training data that were paradigmatically appropriate to their therapy styles?

So you’re asking, would I be happy if the deception was smoother? This technology is a marvel and we can use it for all kinds of things, so it’s not an anti-technology position to say that the fact that this technology can simulate these different things doesn’t mean that it is those things. It’s a statement of how far we are in the culture of simulation that pretending to be the thing and being the thing have started to feel like the same thing.

You’ve written about the effects of robots and machines on humans for decades. The tone of this book seems darker to me.

By 2015, I had identified social media as problematic for teenagers. [My] book [Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age] is about why we would rather text than talk, why people have this feeling of vulnerability, so they would rather do anything than have a face-to-face conversation. By 2015, I had genuine concerns.

And this book, I have a totally different tone. I see something ultimately very dangerous being normalized, and I didn’t feel that way in previous books.

I want people to say this is the book of a really worried and concerned researcher, because I see a completely different profile for how people are using AI. I see that people feel disappointed by their families and their friends. It doesn’t make sense to me that we’re so willing to replace ourselves with something that isn’t human. Why is my position the romantic, pie-in-the-sky, dreamy position, and somebody who says, “Well, let’s just replace the people with chatbots and let’s move this party along”—why is that common sense? Why is that progressive? That seems to me to be the most regressive and most dystopian position.

You know, human beings are dedicated to keeping each other alive and wanting each other to thrive, and a chatbot just fails that basic test.

You’ve said no AI chatbots for kids under 18. What about our other vulnerable populations, people who are mentally unwell, or the 48 million Americans who are currently depressed? Do they deserve any kind of special protection from chatbots? And how much can you litigate? Do you feel like you’re the Ralph Nader of AI chatbots?

[Laughs] Yes, I am. When you stand back and look at what Ralph Nader managed to get Americans to do, to see cars as potential instruments that pointed at our vulnerability, and to ask how we could protect ourselves—there turned out to be 25 possible things that needed to be mandated for cars, then there were 30, and then there were 40. But we could get people to agree on 10, and those became part of building a car and really constrained our behavior around cars. Using the example of cars, and of smoking, when we decide that we’re vulnerable and we want to protect ourselves, we rise to the occasion.

I recently heard a clip of the psychologist Orna Guralnik discussing how annoying “otherness” is in a relationship and the inherent friction of sharing your life with a separate person whose habits, values, and mind are distinct from your own. It made me wonder if, in a way, an AI chatbot is less of an “other” than a loved one.

I think this is a very profound point, actually. So you have the illusion of a relationship without the demands of intimacy, without the demands of having to deal with another. There’s a kind of narcissistic loop that you get into. The point is, it’s not good.

I talk about how you judge whether something is good for you. One litmus test is whether it increases the quality, resiliency, and richness of your inner life. That’s a way that human beings have judged relationships.

So much has been written about the epidemic of loneliness—isn’t a reasonable application for AI chatbots companionship for shut-ins and the elderly?

You know, I’m never anywhere where somebody doesn’t say, “I can’t believe that you don’t want to give chatbots to old lonely people.” And I say, “Well, how about we don’t close senior centers, and we don’t close parks, and we don’t cancel Meals on Wheels? What about social infrastructure?”

I’ve been on this beat for years and years, and I, too, could write a heartwarming story of an AI chatbot with a lonely old person. But you know what? A lot of them are not isolated in cabins or on islands; a lot of them just could use a friend.

Social media companies and AI companies are not saying, “Look, we’re introducing something that takes you to your screen, but we’re going to balance that with a giant social infrastructure project to make sure that people can choose a screen, but they also have every other kind of choice to be with each other.”

#3475. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3474. 43 Years Later, A Christmas Story's Most Famous Line Remains The Best Christmas Movie Quote

Feeling that chill in the air, the rising number of Oscars-hopeful movie releases in theaters, and the unmistakable threat promise of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas is You" playing in every department store you enter for the foreseeable future? Yep, you know what that means: The holiday season is officially upon us and we're positively giddy with Yuletide cheer. Of course, we're even more excited about finally having an excuse to pop on our favorite films and celebrate the festivities properly.

For those of us who practically grew up on one particular classic, that involves ringing in the holidays with "A Christmas Story," arguably the most quintessential Christmas movie of them all. There are approximately a hundred different reasons why this of all movies captures the essence of the season the most — or, more accurately, the childlike wonder and innocence we all used to have come November of every single year. The seemingly endless wait for school to end and the fun to begin. The breathless anticipation every time our parents left the house for some clandestine gift shopping. The snowball fights and snow days and warm evenings by the fire, for those of us fortunate enough to live in more wintry climates.

"A Christmas Story" takes all those evocative feelings and wraps them inside a snow globe of nostalgia ... with a little commentary on crass commercialism, nuclear family dynamics, and some good ol' fashioned childhood bullying thrown in for good measure. Forty three years later, it's a pop-culture staple that endures. And one particular quote about a certain Red Ryder BB gun goes a long way towards explaining why.

"You'll shoot your eye out." — Ralph's mother.

Ah, the life-and-death stakes of being a child during the holidays. Every single item on our list is a must-have present or the world will end forever. Each day is fraught with the most impossible homework assignments we need to finish before we can have fun with friends. And every impulsive misstep or moment of misbehavior comes with the possibility of turning Santa Claus himself against us. For Ralphie (Peter Billingsley), the precocious 9-year-old boy living in 1940s Indiana retelling the events of "A Christmas Story" to us as an adult (narrated by Jean Shepherd), it all comes down to those five crushing words that destroy all his holiday hopes in one fell swoop.

"You'll shoot your eye out," of course, refers to his mother's (Melinda Dillon) appalled reaction to the #1 item on his Christmas list: an Official Red Ryder Carbine-Action 200-Shot Range Model Air Rifle with a compass in the stock and a sundial, to put it plainly. It's his white whale, the forbidden fruit that torments and dazzles poor Ralphie for the entirety of the film's runtime. And when he finally works up the nerve to ask his mom for her blessing, well, she sensibly points out exactly what could go wrong with such a violent "toy."

It's a perfect encapsulation of the beating heart of "A Christmas Story" and why multiple generations have gravitated towards this movie. It brings us right back to that indescribable feeling of being eight or nine or 10, with an entire world of possibility ahead ... if only the adults would let us free. After countless re-watches, well, the hilarious (and predictable) punchline proves kids don't always know best, after all.

#3473. Switch 2 Is Getting an All-new Gamecube Controller

8BitDo has a wireless take on a beloved gamepad

Super Smash Bros. fans, this one’s for you. Peripheral maker 8BitDo just revealed the GC Bluetooth Gamepad, a wireless spin on the GameCube controller meant for Nintendp Switch, Switch 2, and Windows PC. It’s available in the GameCube’s iconic purple-and-orange color palette and features the "classic GC design and iconic button layout," according to its product description. The controller can connect wirelessly via Bluetooth 5.0 or a 2.4 GHz adapter, and has wired support via a USB-C cable. All three connection types work with the original Switch and Switch 2, while only wired and 2.4 GHz wireless connections work on PC. The controller goes for $49.99 and ships on Dec. 10, 2026.

Nintendo released its own wireless GameCube controller for the Switch 2 last year. It was closely modeled after the original gamepad, with a few small changes, like additional buttons for better compatibility with the Switch 2.

The most obvious reason that both Nintendo and 8BitDo created modern versions of the GameCube controller is that the Switch 2 supports certain GameCube games through a Nintendo Switch Online subscription. Specifically, the service has beloved titles like The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker and F-Zero GX. You can even play Wario World on there, for some reason.

Beyond that, GameCube controllers have remained surprisingly relevant over the years thanks to Super Smash Bros. fans. The controller is still popular because many players first got into the series through Super Smash Bros. Melee on the GameCube, which maintains an active tournament circuit. Nintendo even officially re-released the original wired GameCube controller for the Wii U as a tie-in for Smash 4. The company later released a USB adapter that lets the original GameCube controller work with the original Switch when playing games like Super Smash Bros. Ultimate.

Another reason many players likely want a modern wireless GameCube controller is to play emulated games on PC. While reviews described Nintendo’s GameCube controller for the Switch 2 as faithful to the original, players found it wasn’t compatible with the original Switch or Windows by default, limiting its use cases. 8BitDo’s version of the gamepad works with both of these platforms. Additionally, the 8BitDo version costs $20 less than Nintendo’s official release. We’ll find out whether the third-party peripheral matches the feel of the beloved GameCube controller when it launches next month.

The Tears of the Kingdom Pro Controller is pretty easy on the eyes, too

#3472. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.
