#3471. Amazon's Jeff Bezos Clarifies Involvement In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

As exciting as it is that Robert Pattinson has been cast as James Bond, the irony of his 007 movie being overseen by a man who is about as close to a real-life Bond villain as you're likely to get is inescapable. What does Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos know about movies? Well, that remains unclear. But since Amazon bought Bond for an eye-watering sum back in 2025, he is the man who cuts the checks at the end of the day. That means he was always going to have a say in who plays Bond and it seems he was, indeed, intimately involved.

Bezos appeared at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event where he confirmed that he was "heavily involved" in Pattinson's casting (via Twitter/X). "We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on [the Friday before the official announcement was made the following Monday]," he said. "There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists."

.@JeffBezos tells @lizrhoffman he was "heavily involved" in selecting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

"Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous ... but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond." pic.twitter.com/1ro4R8meYO

According to the Amazon founder, the process of whittling down the finalists (let's agree never to use the phrase "down-selected" again) involved carrying out "old-fashioned screen tests" which he described as "interesting." These tests apparently involved "full costumes and real sets and other actors," with Bezos going on to explain how each of the five candidates performed three scenes on-camera. "Then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that," he continued. "By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance. It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director ... we all gravitated toward Rob."

It's interesting to hear Jeff Bezos' recollection of how Robert Pattinson was cast as James Bond. Soon after Amazon made the official announcement, reports emerged that claimed Pattinson wasn't actually director Denis Villeneuve's first choice for Bond. Instead, it seems the director was set on casting "Wake Up Dead Man" and "Disclosure Day" star Josh O'Connor, before the actor chose to take himself out of the process. To hear Bezos tell it, however, all five Bond finalists screen tested and the clear favorite was Pattinson.

Those finalists reportedly comprised O'Connor, Pattinson, "Slow Horses" star Jack Lowden, Callum Turner of the "Fantastic Beasts" films, and the man who will seemingly forever come in second to Pattinson: Nicholas Hoult. Rather than Pattinson being a second choice, in Bezos' recollection he simply came out on top after the screen tests and the decision was about as close to unanimous as you can get.

With all that in mind, it remains unclear just how the final days of the casting process unfolded. Was O'Connor still in the running on that Friday Bezos and co. watched the screen tests? How late, exactly, did Pattinson enter the process, considering he reportedly had to escape his "The Batman: Part III" contract ahead of his Bond casting? What is clear at this point is that the Amazon founder was right there alongside producers and Villeneuve to oversee the final decision.

Interestingly enough, during his Semafor event comments Jeff Bezos also claimed that Robert Pattinson didn't start out as the favorite for "Bond 26." "Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous," he said. "Like, maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond."

Indeed, Pattinson's 007 casting breaks a 60-year tradition of casting relative unknowns as the legendary spy. As such, you can appreciate why the producers were hesitant at first. Ever since "Dr. No" launched cinema's most enduring franchise back in 1962, audiences have gotten used to seeing a fresh face in the role with each new recasting. But Pattinson's star power is actually one of the reasons he could be the best Bond yet. The last few entries in the franchise haven't been the most impressive, and the "Primetime" star will surely help restore a sense of prestige to a saga that's felt quite stale for some time. That's to say nothing of his considerable acting talent, which will no doubt immediately convince the naysayers the moment they see any footage from the film.

That certainly seems to have been the case with Bezos and the gang, who evidently felt Pattinson was a cut above the other Bond hopefuls after seeing his screen test. It remains to be seen what sort of influence the Amazon founder will have over Denis Villeneuve's movie during production, but let's hope he's too distracted by world domination to interfere too much.

As a child of the early 2000s, I grew up obsessed with Gilmore Girls and Gossip Girl. These remarkable teen shows were irresistible, and they are how I was introduced to Jared Padalecki and Leighton Meester. So, you can imagine my excitement when I learned that these actors would be leading the rom-com, Guarding Stars, on the 2026 Christmas movie schedule together. So, I had to ask about how they bonded over their time on shows like Gilmore Girls and Gossip Girl, and Padalecki’s G-oriented response hilariously surprised me.

When I brought all this up to Jared Padalecki, who plays actor Jack Stapleton in Guarding Stars, he said he did speak to Meester about their time on The CW and their work on the “G-titled girl shows,” as Padalecki affectionately called them. Elaborating on that hilarious point, the Supernatural star said:

Yeah, we did talk about it here and there. We didn't get into deep, deep detail. But yeah, I also joke that I was in Gilmore Girls; she was in Gossip Girl. Then there's Golden Girls. We were all on the double G titled girl shows. Well, I didn't get to be on Golden Girls, but I wish.

Well, I certainly didn’t see this hilarious point coming. While I’ve always been entertained by the fact that both Jared Padalecki and Leighton Meester were on maybe two of the three most famous [insert name that starts with G] Girl(s) shows around, I didn’t think he’d bring it up. I also didn’t think he’d say he wanted to be on Golden Girls, but now I wish that could have happened somehow.

Anyway, getting back to the Gossip Girl and Gilmore Girls vets working together, Padalecki said their similar experiences of getting their break on major television programs did help them bond on set. In fact, as they filmed Guarding Stars, which is a Christmas flick on the 2026 movie schedule, in the cold, they found themselves discussing how the industry has evolved with some of their other co-stars:

But we did talk about it and just how the industry in general has changed. Especially, there'd be scenes where it was too cold to wait outside in between takes, so they'd have a warming hut for us or a warming room, and having Andie MacDowell there to talk about when she had started and the differences and this and that, and so we would bond about it.

Yeah, this book-to-screen adaptation of Katherine Center’s The Bodyguard is full of veteran actors. I can only imagine the conversations Padalecki, Meester and MacDowell, who plays Padalecki’s mom in the movie, had. Speaking more to that point, the actor told me that he and the Gossip Girl star's similar TV history did really help them work together:

But I think there was just more than talking about it. There was just an understanding when we got to set that she's a technician and she's talented, and she's done hundreds of hours of work. And I think hopefully she thought the same me, so we just hit the ground running. It wasn't like, ‘No, here's how you hit a mark, and here's how you find the lens.’ Like, I knew she knew; she knew I knew. It's like, ‘Cool, let's play. Let's see what the words bring us.’

So, the double-G connection, if you will, really served them well on this. While Meester and Padalecki were never on the same shows, they both broke big through projects that aired on The CW, and having that background helped them get off to a great start in Guarding Stars.

Now, in this new G project the two actors star in, Padalecki plays an actor, and Meester is his bodyguard. However, to maintain their cover with his parents, they have to fake date. It’s a very fun, wholesome, and action-packed movie that’s well worth the time. And if you’re a fan of the “double G-titled girl shows,” you really won’t want to miss it.

With that said, Guarding Stars is available to stream with a Netflix subscription. And if you’d like to stream “the double G-titled girl shows,” you can catch Gilmore Girls and Golden Girls with either a Disney+ or Hulu subscription, and Gossip Girl is streaming for those with an HBO Max subscription.

#3469. Virginia Feito on the Film Adaptation of Her Novel ‘Victorian Psycho’

The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.- Martin McDonagh

When I finished editing my second novel, Victorian Psycho, I could not imagine we would be shooting the film adaptation the following year, mere months after the book’s publication. Generally, making a movie is one big miracle produced by an amalgamation of thousands of other tiny miracles. But when I met Zach Wigon, I understood that this was a joyfully tenacious person who was going to make this movie if it cost him his life.

I decided then to undertake this journey that would take me metaphorically to Hollywood but geographically to a county just outside of Dublin, where we would recreate the Ensor House of my novel. Among film stars, an Irish crew, and (rumored) ticks, the adaptation of Victorian Psycho—based on my screenplay, which is based on my novel, which is based on my ego, I guess—was born. Throughout the shoot I kept a sort of pseudo diary in order to remember every surreal detail from which I still haven’t recovered. I’ve chosen to reproduce some of it here.

Director Zach Wigon and producer Lisa Kelly call me from the set on the first day of shooting (Zach and I have agreed I won’t visit the set until after the first week so the cast and crew can acclimate without me hovering over them, because I am an intense fame whore, and also, I suppose, to signal I’m not important enough to pull a P.L. Travers and attempt to boycott the movie).

Over the phone, the producer says she can’t wait to meet in person. I tell her I’m underwhelming.

They promise to send me the dailies. I spend all day waiting for the dailies. The dailies never come.

At around 9 p.m., I spiral because I don’t know whether to celebrate with Champagne or KFC. I decide to have both.

I finally get the dailies. I fall in love with Maika Monroe’s character so hard it’s like I have an obsessive crush circa 2006 whose Facebook photos I’m compulsively looking at. But in this case it’s the same scene throughout five almost identical takes of Maika calling a 10-year-old boy a little idiot.

Over the phone, Zach mentions concerns about a specific scene because we don’t have the budget for that many extras. I get carried away and suggest shipping over a whole battalion of free extras from Spain because, in my head, it’s going to be me and my friends, drunk and decked out in period clothing like we’re at a cheesy bachelorette party. One friend starts making childcare arrangements and another cancels her Holter monitor appointment so she can come to the shoot. What could go wrong?

I am informed we are probably no longer going to need the extras, and I feel a huge wave of relief as I uninvite my excited friends. I pack a suitcase for Ireland. It weighs 57 pounds.

I have a steak on the plane to Dublin at, like, 3 p.m., because when you’re flying business and somebody offers you steak, you take it.

The hotel room is wonderful, but I jokingly tell Zach over the phone that it’s on a first floor, so someone might crawl up and break in through the window and rape me, and he laughs at first but then is concerned and tells me to request a room on a higher floor, and I tell him it was a joke, but it wasn’t really.

I fill up the hotel room bathtub and call reception for a glass of red wine because I am a queen and I am queening. The glass doesn’t come, so in my anxious impatience I attempt to open a bottle of red wine sitting above the minibar. The cork crumbles because I’ve never understood how to use a corkscrew—like the compass in math class, I just faked my way through it my entire life and hoped for the best. So I call reception for another glass of red wine. They bring me all the glasses of wine and also properly uncork the bottle, and I watch Seinfeld in the bathtub while I drink red wine. I get drunk and paint my nails.

I arrive on set slightly Bromazepamed. It is extremely surreal to exist in a set labeled “Mr. Pounds’s Bedroom.” I am used to living in the fictional world inside my head but not used to it becoming more real than real life itself.

Maika hugs me when we meet, and I swallow a sob and refrain from smelling her hair (partly because it is, in fact, a wig). Everyone on set appears so happy to meet me, I suspect a Good Bye, Lenin! situation in which I have been diagnosed with cancer and for some reason the cast and crew all know but I don’t know. This isn’t the plot of Good Bye, Lenin!, but you’ll know what I mean if you’ve seen it.

Zach asks me to read the VOs in every scene, which means I’m in the scene with Ruth Wilson, Jason Isaacs, and Maika, and I’m about to have a stroke.

Jason eats for real in every single take and has already gulped down seven sausage rolls, so if I fuck up my VO, I will kill myself.

Suddenly experiencing fiction collectively feels very superior to experiencing it privately. This does not bode well for the rest of my career as a novelist.

There is a scene in a cramped drawing room in which I must read the VO, but I’m supposed to hide from the camera, so I crawl on all fours behind an antique couch and grovel my way around the room while the boom op steps on my hands. I secretly think the boom op hates me because I’m always in his way and have an irritating habit of apologizing when he slams into me.

I start developing Irish inflections, so I say it, “I start developing Irish inflections,” but the Irish seem happy about it, so I pursue it.

Jason Isaacs starts doing card tricks between takes because Jason Isaacs is actually magic and also indefatigable. Only one thing could ever defeat Jason Isaacs, and it’s the ghost allegedly living on the third floor.

Even though Zach asked me to oversee the second unit, I don’t think anyone believes I’m actually going to do this—and between you and me, I don’t really even know what a second unit is. It doesn’t help I can’t concentrate on what we’re shooting because we’re in the middle of the woods and someone said there were ticks, so I’m wrapping Sellotape around my ankles, hoping this way they won’t be able to crawl up my legs.

Like your worst trauma, I insert myself into the movie forever via a small cameo. I literally just have to stand in a wig while I smile and nod, but I do it in such a way that I ruin every single take. “Just smile…like a normal person,” the second-unit director says. I reason Zach can just cut me out of the movie, and I will only have wasted everybody’s time and money. There are worse things, like smiling normally but having no cameo. I cope by chewing on another Bromazepam and another chocolate bar. (Every morning I take the chocolate bar from the hotel minibar. It will invariably become an asset in the long afternoons on set, kind of like in prison or high school.)

I change hotel rooms because I have developed an intense FOMO with which I’m always fearing there is a better hotel room for the same price somewhere in the vicinity. This FOMO is also rampant on set between the different units—in the first unit, you have the cinematographer, Nico Aguilar, laughing in the sunlight, talking about color palettes, while in the second unit, we’re shooting clocks and screaming at each other because we still have 17 establishing shots to go.

Anyway, I change hotel rooms, and the new room is so superior to my previous room it’s like an entirely new hotel. I consider changing hotel rooms further. Perhaps I can somehow upgrade my way into a presidential suite.

My parents visit the set. My dad peers over his glasses at the fake lobster cake, and when I tell him the toilets are in trailers, he sighs gravely.

Jason Isaacs convinces my dad to take up tennis again even though my dad’s not supposed to play tennis after his seven hernias. But my dad is so inspired by this actor, who is not a doctor but whose performance in The Patriot my dad can’t help but praise at least once a month, that he will immediately start playing tennis again upon his return to Spain, and whatever medical issues arise henceforth shall all be Jason Isaacs’s fault.

At the Shelbourne restaurant that night, my mom tells the sommelier how she can’t drink red wine anymore because it makes her anxious, and he kneels on the floor beside her and places a hand on his heart as if she were confiding something intimate to him like her fear of death.

Suddenly, real life feels less real than fictional life.

Obama is visiting Dublin and he’s booked the entire floor, so he essentially kicks me out of the Shelbourne (probably to stay in the JFK Suite next door to my room, which is disappointingly predictable), so I go to The Hoxton, because what is life if you’re not constantly changing hotel rooms? The Hoxton is really lovely, but I get OCD about the light bulbs in the room because they appear mismatched, so I ask housekeeping to change them, but they claim not to have any extra light bulbs, which sounds suspect—like, what do they do if a light bulb suddenly goes out? Do they just never replace it?

We end the shoot at 5 a.m. I am wearing a thick puffer coat and a thermal T-shirt and a furry hat, plus fur-lined boots over my Sellotaped ankles, although I wonder, If ticks can survive this temperature, they kind of deserve to live off my blood. Nobody else seems as concerned about the cold as me, but then again, most of them are Irish.

Sadly, when we wrap, we are all so exhausted everyone races to clean up and leave, and it is sort of anticlimactic. I don’t know what I was expecting, but balloons falling from the skies did flash through my mind.

In the car on the way to our respective quarters, Zach and I look out the window, wide-eyed, like kidnapped children. Zach starts discussing a new project for us. I wonder if he is a sociopath.

I type this over a year later, sitting at my desk in Madrid, striving to work on my next novel. I feel empty inside knowing there is no car to pick me up and take me to set and thereby escape reality for extended periods of time, until set becomes reality and reality becomes a limbo in which you wait for said reality.

I am working on a novel, but also on four new scripts. I hope to return to reality someday.

#3467. GTA 6's Completely Unrealistic Mountains Had to Be in the Game, Rockstar Says

GTA 6 takes some liberties with its world around Vice City

If you’ve ever spent time in and around Miami, Grand Theft Auto 6 is bound to delight you. Rockstar Games spared no expense in bringing the diverse world of Florida to life in digital form. Walk down the street in Vice City, and you’re sure to find an approximation of a bar you’ve actually been to. Head to the Leonida Keys, and you’ll find rows of houses on stilts. The attention to detail is impressive, but it also makes one odd detail about the map a little odd.

Go all the way north in Leonida, right up to Lummox County, and you’ll be able to go hiking and hunting in the mountains. As any Floridian will tell you, that’s not exactly reflective of the real Florida’s topography. Why take such a major creative liberty there when so much else about Leonida is grounded in realism? In an interview with Polygon, Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson explained why GTA 6 takes players to the mountains.

Nelson said that one of the biggest challenges the team faced when designing the game was figuring out the map. Rockstar’s map team began working on the game in 2015, Nelson said, well before anyone else at the studio. While creating another city was easy enough for a team that has mastered that art, expanding to surrounding Florida locales was a tougher proposition. That’s because Florida is a very flat state.

The problem with depicting it as is, though, is that GTA players likely would have some expectations about what should be in a modern GTA map. GTA 5, for instance, built off of Los Angeles to create Los Santos. Because of that, the map has a lot of variety in elevation. That wouldn’t be possible if Leonida stuck too close to reality, so Rockstar ultimately decided to include some mountains to keep GTA 6 a little more consistent with GTA 5.

Though it may not be accurate, it’s a welcome addition to the map. As fun as it is to drive around Vice City, weaving around the same highways can get old. Lummox County offers a lot more open space for off-roading, biking, and other activities that just wouldn’t be possible in a city. For instance, when I found a bicycle perched atop a hill, I found myself racing down a natural BMX course that was built into the world. Every time I head up to Lummox County, it feels like I’m on vacation.

Crucially, it’s also the best date spot in the entire game. You can take Jason and Lucia out on impromptu dates throughout GTA 6, letting the couple play some mini-golf together or blow off steam at a shooting range. One of my favorite play sessions so far simply happened when I got the two in a truck and took them up north to a part of the map I’d never seen. We got out when we found a hiking trail and wound up stumbling into some ruins high up on a hill. It was a peaceful moment of discovery that the two got to share together. Moments like that are what make GTA 6 special, and Leonida’s intricate design is the thing that powers it all.

Rockstar’s magnum opus searches for love and catharsis in desperate times — and finds them

#3466. 10 Years Ago Today: Hailee Steinfeld Starred In One Of The Best Coming-Of-Age Movies Of All Time

Actor Hailee Steinfeld broke out in the Coen Brothers' 2010 Western film "True Grit" as the precocious Mattie Ross, who speaks like she's wise beyond her years but lacks the experience that brings true wisdom. We at /Film consider Steinfeld as Mattie the greatest performance in any Coens movie, which is no small feat.

Nominated for an Academy Award at only 14 years old, it would've been easy for Steinfeld's career to have peaked there. But she has kept challenging herself with music, voice acting, and plenty of new movies, and one of her best is absolutely writer/director Kelly Fremon Craig's coming-of-age film "The Edge of Seventeen."

After a premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, "The Edge of Seventeen" hit theaters on November 18, 2016. It takes its title from the Stevie Nicks song yet applies it more literally to this story about a 17-year-old girl. The acerbic, awkward, and unpopular Nadine Franklin (Steinfeld) has lost the two people in the world who understand her. One, her father, Tom (Eric Keenleyside), who died a few years prior of a heart attack. Now, her best friend, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has started dating Nadine's older brother Darian (Blake Jenner), whom Nadine loathes for having their mother Mona's (Kyra Sedgewick) favor and being so effortlessly beloved and successful.

"I've gotta spend the rest of my life with myself," Nadine says while drunk. We all realize that and then come to terms with it at some point. Nadine's story fits in the gap between the realization and the coming to terms. Speaking as someone who was the same age as Nadine was in 2016, and saw "The Edge of Seventeen" in his senior year of high school, few coming-of-age movies depict awkward adolescence in the 2010s more honestly.

Critics compared "The Edge of Seventeen" to a modern John Hughes movie, as did Hailee Steinfeld herself. In 2016, she explained to Entertainment Weekly that she hoped that the movie could reflect her generation's teen years back at them while still being timeless, in the same way "Sixteen Candles" and "The Breakfast Club" — films made for 1980s kids — still resonated with her (someone born in 1996).

But "The Edge of Seventeen" doesn't soften itself by looking to echoes of older movies instead of real life. The film begins with Nadine marching up to her history teacher, Mr. Bruner (Woody Harrelson) in his classroom, announcing she's planning to die by suicide and wants someone to know first. That opening makes you think you're in for a movie about an inspirational teacher who talks a depressed student back from the edge and shows them why life is worth living. Well, not quite.

We see, as Mr. Bruner immediately recognizes, this is Nadine being dramatic. "I don't want to take up a ton of your time" she says right off, which is her first lie. The movie then rewinds (with the help of some voiceover from Nadine, though that fades pretty quickly) before catching back up with this cold open. What led to her current situation? Nadine accidentally sent a text to her crush, Nick (Alexander Calvert), describing very explicitly how she wants to hook up with him.

That complements one of the best bits of writing in the film, one that definitely helped it speak to my younger self. Nadine has a lot of movie-typical teenage boy qualities: she doesn't fit in, dresses in baggy sweatshirts, has a hopeless crush she never talks to, makes sex jokes while mistaking vulgarity for wit, etc.

During the "Edge of Seventeen" press tour, Kelly Fremon Craig and producer James L. Brooks spoke with /Film. Craig cited some "life-altering" writing advice from Brooks, that she needed to ask herself, "What is this movie saying about life?" I would answer that "The Edge of Seventeen" is about how, when you're a teenager, your problems seem like the whole world and that part of growing up is realizing others — even people who irritate you everyday (as Nadine's mom and brother do to her) — are dealing with their own pain.

Upon its release, "The Edge of Seventeen" saw only modest financial success, grossing $19 million in theaters against its $9 million budget. A spin-off TV series ordered by YouTube Red ultimately didn't move forward, either. I would also argue the film's anticipated reputation as "definitive teen movie of the 2010s" was overshadowed by Greta Gerwig's "Lady Bird," which came out the following year and hits similar beats while finding both great financial success and critical acclaim. Not that "The Edge of Seventeen" has been lost to time or anything, though.

In that aforementioned /Film interview, Craig claimed, "If [Hailee Steinfeld] didn't exist, the movie wouldn't exist," because she brought a sui generis quality to Nadine as she once did to Mattie Ross. The two would work together again on the "Transformers" spin-off film "Bumblebee," where Steinfeld starred and Craig performed rewrites. "Bumblebee" often feels like "The Edge of Seventeen" but with Transformers included.

A couple of times in "The Edge of Seventeen," Nadine looks up to the sky and asks if God is even paying attention to her. Perhaps it's not surprising that when Craig directed another coming-of-age film, she adapted Judy Blume's classic novel "Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret."

Ebenzer was at the top of the box office when it arrived in theaters, but the book to screen adaptation didn't make that much money compared to Depp's past projects. Over on the Naughty But Nice Substack, writer Rob Shuter quoted an alleged industry insider, who spoke about how the movie's performance may influence the future of Johnny Depp's career. In their words:

This was Johnny’s test, and he got a C. That’s not good enough for a studio looking to spend a fortune on a franchise. The problem is, it wasn’t a complete disaster. If the movie had totally bombed, everyone could walk away and move on. Instead, these middle-of-the-road numbers leave Hollywood with a difficult decision.

At the time of writing this story, Ebenzer has made $43.4 million on a reported budget of $38 million. Johnny Depp took a huge pay cut to keep at number low, but it wasn't enough to reach huge box office numbers of previous projects like the Pirates of the Caribbean movies. If this source is to be believed, the powers at Hollywood might not be inclined to give him major gigs following how Ti West's new movie did.

Ebenezer's cast has plenty of familiar faces, but Depp has been front and center of the movie's promotional tour. He even showed up at San Diego Comic-Con dressed as Scrooge. Fans have been wondering if the actor might return as Captain Jack Sparrow in another Pirates movie, but according to the same source, that might be less likely after Ebenezer. They claimed:

Pirates is the ultimate prize for Johnny, but Hollywood needs to know audiences still want to see him. Nostalgia alone won’t sell hundreds of millions of dollars in tickets.

We should probably take these quotes with a grain of salt, but it should be interesting to see where/if Johnny Depp appears in another major film production. He returned to acting in Jeanne du Barry, but that was a French film produced outside of the Hollywood machine. While he's got plenty of beloved movies on his resume, it's unclear if moviegoing audiences can get past the Amber Heard ordeal and still want to show up in theaters to see him on the big screen.

Ebenezer is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll have to see how much money it makes deeper into its theatrical run, as well as what projects Johnny Depp signs on for next.

#3464. A Survivor of Alleged Sex Abuse at Miss Hall’s School in the Berkshires Speaks Out.

At 6:04 on the morning of March 29, 2024, my phone lit up with a long text from Matt Rutledge. The head of school had called him the night before, he wrote, while he was watching television with his wife. He was on paid administrative leave, his school email was frozen, and he assumed this was about him and me. He called what he had done to me a relationship. He didn’t regret his feelings for me. Could I call him when his wife was out of the house?

I was thirty-seven years old. I was a few weeks out from my partnership interview at a New York law firm. I had a husband and a three-year-old son. I spend my working life telling clients which sentences will look bad in discovery. I read that text twice, and my first thought was, How can I help him?

He had spent years teaching me to use his word for it. It was never a relationship. He groomed me, he exploited me, and he raped me.

Vanity Fair has written about that morning before. Evgenia Peretz opened “Girls, Interrupted” with that text in January 2025, and she went back to Miss Hall’s last fall after the investigation came out. In March, Dan Adler covered the indictment. This time I’m telling it myself.

Later that morning an email arrived from an attorney in Boston. Subject line: “Reaching out about Miss Hall’s School.” I didn’t open it right away. I didn’t need to. Some part of me had been composing that email in my head since I was a teenager. The attorney represented a woman named Melissa Fares, a Miss Hall’s alumna who had been there a few years after me. I had never heard her name.

She had heard mine. Years earlier, older girls at the school had told her about me. She held on to my name, and when she went to a lawyer she remembered it. By then I had married and changed it, and they found me anyway.

I called Matt and asked. “Who is Melissa?” There was a pause long enough to hear him decide something, then a sigh, and then he told me he had had sex with Melissa while she was a student.

Here is what I did next, and I’d ask you to withhold judgment. I told him I would call the lawyer, find out what she had, and report back.

That’s what twenty-two years of being groomed looks like at a desk in Midtown. You don’t make a decision. The decision was made for you a long time ago, in a dorm room, and you’re simply carrying it out.

I did call the lawyer. And when I heard my own voice say “I’m not ready to talk to you, I want to talk to Melissa,” I think that was the first sentence in two decades that I said entirely for myself.

Melissa called that afternoon. I don’t remember how she started. I remember what I said before she got far.

“I’ve been waiting for your call for twenty years.”

I meant it literally. Some part of me had always known I wasn’t the only one. I just couldn’t go looking. I could only wait to be found.

Hilary Simon and Melissa Fares, photographed in Far Rockaway, New York, 2025.

She told me her story, and I heard my own memories come out of a stranger’s mouth. He called her “Little One.” He called me “Little One.” He took her to the same hotel in Northampton. He told her he would kill himself if she ever told anyone, which is a thing he had also told me, more than once, in nearly the same words. He had made himself the center of her emotional world before he ever touched her. He had a script.

For twenty years he had me believing that what happened was singular, and that it was my fault. By the end of that call it was a pattern, and I was a data point. I was not special. It is a strange thing to grieve, not being special to the person who hurt you. I grieved it anyway.

After more than three decades teaching at that school, he resigned the same day.

I arrived at Miss Hall’s, an all-girls boarding school in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in the fall of 2001. I was fourteen, homesick, and like every other girl my age, positive I was more grown up than I was.

Rutledge had been teaching history there for a decade. He was a big man with a booming voice, married with two daughters. He lived with his family in a school-owned house across the street from the main entrance. He used to cut the lunch line announcing himself as “Mr. Wonderful.” Girls talked about him like he was a minor deity. They also mentioned, in the breezy way teenagers mention terrible things, that he had a type.

Some evenings, he was one of the adults who did bed checks in the dorms. The others always stood in the doorway. He came in and sat on the edge of my bed.

By the next fall he was my advisor and my cross-country coach. There was no door at that school he couldn’t open. On the long drives to meets, he told me to sit next to him in the school van. He called me his copilot. The rest of the team sat behind us. He would put his hand on my upper thigh, or pull me close until our legs were touching. I watched the Berkshire hills go by and tried not to look down.

That was the first line he crossed. I was fifteen. After that he crossed them one at a time until there were none left. He kept abusing me for years after I graduated.

From the outside, those years looked like a success story.

I went to college and then law school. I became a civil defense attorney. I got married. I had a son. I was good at my job.

I could find the unanswered email in ten thousand pages of discovery. The report nobody followed up on. I couldn’t open my own file.

When I tell this story, people ask me some version of the same question. How did nobody notice?

In the late 1990s, years before I ever set foot on Miss Hall’s campus, a student stood up at a school meeting and said Mr. Rutledge was having sex with another student. The school suspended her for the rest of the year, barred her from graduation and made her write him an apology letter. He kept teaching.

On my graduation day, Rutledge kissed me and told me that he loved me. A classmate told a staff member, who reported it to the administration. In a memo, Rutledge admitted telling me he loved me but said “[it was] not a romantic expression.” He denied the kiss. They took his word for it. No one called me or my parents.

A few years later, after a family reported that he had made advances toward their daughter, the head of school at that time, Jeannie Norris, put a warning to Rutledge in writing. “This isn’t the 70s or the 80s,” she wrote. “Society has no stomach for any kind of inappropriate behavior between adults and girls or teachers and students.” She was worried about the school’s reputation, and about his. In the letter she said the incident had “the potential for seriously damaging the School and your [Rutledge’s] reputation.” He was not fired.

Over the years that followed Rutledge was made chair of the history department and collected faculty honors. More than one person gave the school my name as a girl he had singled out. Nobody ever called me. In June 2023, I heard another alumna tried to raise concerns about him with the head of school at that time. He was still teaching nine months later, when Melissa reported him.

In August 2025 Miss Hall’s published the results of an outside investigation it had commissioned from Aleta Law. The investigators substantiated grooming and abuse by Rutledge involving at least five students. They found school leadership had been warned about him over the years and hadn’t acted. Staff members told investigators they had suspected him and kept quiet, some because they feared retaliation, others because they assumed no one in charge would listen.

It went beyond Rutledge. The investigation found that seven other Miss Hall’s employees had engaged in sexual misconduct with students, dating back to the 1940s. Eight adults across eighty plus years. That’s a culture of abuse.

A Berkshire County grand jury has since indicted Norris on a charge of reckless endangerment of a child. She has pleaded not guilty. Another former Miss Hall’s teacher has been indicted for assault with intent to rape and indecent assault and two counts battery of a student. He has also pleaded not guilty.

I read all sixty pages of the Aleta Law report in one sitting. Nothing in it surprised me. It still knocked the air out of me to see my adolescence reduced to numbered findings.

Melissa arrived at Miss Hall’s in 2007, two years after I left.

People sometimes call us friends. That’s true, but it’s a small word for it. I call her my sister survivor.

I wouldn’t be writing this if Melissa hadn’t gone first. She went to the school alone. In April 2024, she told her story publicly. A few weeks later, I told mine. Then other women came forward. They said Rutledge had abused them too.

In October 2024, the Berkshire district attorney said he didn’t believe he could charge Rutledge. In Massachusetts, the age of consent is sixteen. Under the law, a teacher could claim that a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old student had consented.

Melissa and I set out to change the law. We testified at the State House and knocked on every door that would open. Enough Abuse, a Massachusetts nonprofit, had been fighting for this for years. Two national advocacy groups, World Without Exploitation and I Have The Right To, stood with us. Representatives Leigh Davis and John Lawn pushed for it in the House, and Senator Joan Lovely added it to the state budget. In July, Governor Healey signed the Trusted Adults Act.

In Massachusetts, it is now a felony for a teacher or coach to have sex with a student under eighteen.

Melissa and I spoke at the signing ceremony. I stood right next to the governor and thought about the girl in the front seat of the school van, with her teacher’s hand on her leg.

While we were working on the law, Massachusetts State Police and a new team of prosecutors in the Berkshire district attorney’s office had reopened the investigation into Rutledge. Melissa and I testified before a grand jury. In March, he was indicted on three counts of rape.

In April, he was arraigned. It was the first time Melissa and I faced him together. In the courtroom, I handed out orange heart stickers. Orange is Melissa’s favorite color. When we saw Rutledge, we both went numb. We had learned to do that as girls, when going somewhere else in our heads was the only way through. He pleaded not guilty.

I looked back at the benches. They were full of orange. Teachers from Miss Hall’s, people from the community, alumnae across generations. I had been alone with this since I was fifteen. That day, a whole room sat behind us. Afterward, Melissa told reporters that for the first time, she held the power in a room with him. I felt it too.

This month, nine years after #MeToo took off, a jury in London convicted Russell Brand of one rape and three sexual assaults. A judge sentenced him to ten and a half years in prison. His crimes went back to 2004. Brand’s attorneys argued the women had waited too long to be believed. I waited twenty years. Delay is often the most ordinary fact in these cases.

In the midterms, Ohio elected Amy Acton governor. A few weeks before the vote, her opponent’s campaign ran an ad in which her estranged mother called her a liar. Acton’s stepfather had been charged with raping her when she was a child. Republicans and Democrats both condemned the ad. She won anyway.

I watched the returns on election night and thought about the girls at Miss Hall’s who told the truth and were called liars. Survivors get called liars all the time. We almost never get to watch one win.

Tarana Burke knew survivors weren’t being believed long before most people were listening. She started saying “me too” in 2006 to reach Black girls who had survived sexual violence, more than ten years before it became a hashtag. Every survivor who spoke after her made it a little easier for the next one.

In November 2024, a Cornell student told campus police and the Title IX office that she had been gang-raped at a fraternity house weeks earlier. No one has been charged. Cornell’s president set up a task force on sexual assault, but he later admitted he never checked how her case ended.

When I read that, I was back at Miss Hall’s on graduation day, waiting for a phone call that nobody made.

The Epstein survivors know that silence too. For decades, powerful people looked away. Last year survivors pushed Congress to pass a law requiring the Justice Department to release its Epstein files. Millions of pages came out. There have been no arrests in the United States.

I’m still hopeful. Survivors everywhere keep coming forward, and some of the people in charge are finally acting. My body knew what Rutledge had done to me long before I let myself say it aloud. I didn’t have the words. Survivors today do, and they have each other. Melissa found me.

The criminal case against Rutledge isn’t over. His lawyer has asked a judge to dismiss all charges. We don’t know yet whether there will be a trial. Whatever the judge decides, I’ve already reached my own verdict. I’m healing and Rutledge doesn’t get a say in that.

For most of my life, I carried shame that was never mine. He handed it to me. Every adult who looked away handed me a little more.

Predators don’t work alone. Someone always sees something. In the movie Spotlight, a lawyer says that if it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a village to abuse one. My village saw. The people in charge did nothing.

I’ve given the shame back. It belongs to him, and to the people who could have stopped him.

If you are a survivor and you are still carrying shame, you can put it down.

Borrow my courage if you need it. Melissa lent me hers.

Neither Matthew Rutledge nor Jean Norris responded to Vanity Fair for the original story, and neither of them has made direct statements to the press. Norris, through her attorney, claimed not to know that Rutledge abused students.

#3463. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Best Storyline Redeems A Controversial Peter Jackson Idea

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching Season 3, Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

Over halfway into its run, it's clear "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 is spectacular whenever Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is on-screen. Indeed, this season is for the baddies, with the Dark Lord's menacing Nazgnagôl making their grand entrance and a thrilling civil war brewing in Númenor.

But it's not all doom and gloom, as Season 3 also introduces the brightest light of hope in Middle-earth: the elven golden retriver Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). From the moment he shows up, it feels like he's been a part of the show from the start, fitting in perfectly as a strong, funny, flirty elf who has excellent chemistry with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark). Celeborn is the ultimate wife guy, and his relationship with Galadriel is the best romance we've seen in a Middle-earth adventure to date.

Nevertheless, there's trouble in Valinor for these two, as Celeborn has competition for Galadriel's heart. No, not Robert Aramayo's Elrond (despite them sharing a kiss in Season 2 to distract the orcs holding Galadriel captive), but Sauron, the Dark Lord on his dark throne in the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

That's right: "The Rings of Power" Season 3 has finally turned "The Lord of the Rings" into a romantasy story, placing a love triangle at the heart of the saga of the One Ring. And while J.R.R. Tolkien purists may scoff at this, the show's love triangle is so good that it redeems the controversial romances from Peter Jackson's otherwise beloved "Lord of the Rings" films.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films are the most widely celebrated fantasy movies of all time and changed the genre forever. As such, it's easy nowadays to forget that Jackson's trilogy stirred up its fair share of controversy upon its initial release. After all, as faithful as they were to J.R.R. Tolkien's original books overall, those films also made some big alterations. That includes erasing the Scouring of The Shire from "The Return of the King" and removing characters like Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel, in addition to introducing a prominent love triangle.

In Jackson's movies, to jog your memory, a respectable amount of time is spent on Éowyn (Miranda Otto) falling in love with Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), with even King Théoden (Bernard Hill) buying into their match and congratulating Éowyn on finding a good and honest man. Meanwhile, Aragorn keeps thinking about Arwen (Liv Tyler), who is about to leave Middle-earth for Valinor. In fact, the original plan was for Arwen to be at Helm's Deep alongside Éowyn and Aragorn in "The Two Towers," which presumably would've fueled their love triangle even further.

Things get even worse in Jackson's "The Hobbit" films. There, he and co-writers Philippa Boyens and Fran Walsh introduce Tauriel (Evangeline Lilly), an elf who develops romantic feelings for the dwarf Kili (Aidan Turner). In that case, it's Legolas (Orlando Bloom) who rounds out the love triangle, as he's still racist towards dwarves at the time.

Neither of these Middle-earth love triangles really work (especially not the latter), so it's hard not to be skeptical of "The Rings of Power" introducing yet another one. And yet, this ends up being the most compelling aspect of Season 3.

There are two things that make the love triangle in "The Rings of Power" work. The first is that the show is very clearly in on the joke, with Sauron often behaving like a teenager when it comes to his borderline hilarious fixation on Galadriel. That he even goes to the trouble of disguising himself as Galadriel and kissing Celeborn to get information out of him shows Sauron is not beyond being a little bi-curious.

Then there's the fact that the series has been building to this since Season 1, starting with Galadriel slowly falling for Sauron in disguise as Halbrand and being seduced by his promises of power. By the time Season 3 rolls along, she still has complicated feelings for him, as evidenced by her dreams and visions of Sauron waking up in bed next to her. Thus, when Celeborn re-enters her life, and Galadriel sees both men in front of her, there's a tiny bit of hesitation on her part.

And yet, Season 3 never suggests that Galadriel would actually leave her husband for the Dark Lord. Instead, it juxtaposes Sauron's jealousy with Celeborn's confidence. Specifically, in Episodes 5 and 6, Sauron gets visibly flustered when Celeborn talks about how much Galadriel loves him. In the end, it works just as well as the incredible romances in J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, proving that Middle-earth is not devoid of effective romantic storytelling.

Heck, the scene in Episode 6where Celeborn talks about making the elven smith that Sauron has been looking for tell him the secrets of the rings, just so he can hear about every minute the smith spent with Galadriel, is arguably the most romantic TV scene of 2026. Stream Season 3 on Prime Video, and see for yourself.

#3462. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3459. Meta's VR Glasses Could Be The Future Of Home Viewing (But They Probably Won't)

In stark contrast to the dire straits that the movie theater industry was in just a few years ago, 2026 has been especially encouraging to those of us who adore going to the movies. A big part of why that's changed lies in the industry's embrace of unique Premium Large Formats, with numerous releases this year having been shown in formats like IMAX, 4DX, Screen X, Dolby Cinema, and so on. Along the way, screening on celluloid (70mm in particular) have become a draw unto themselves, and some cities are home to even more specialized formats, among them Las Vegas' immersive Sphere and the Cosm experience. And while the biggest draw to movie theaters will always be good films, it's clear that audiences also enjoy an experience they can't get elsewhere.

As usual, however, the tech industry isn't far behind to try and stoke the competition between theaters and home viewing. While most consumers have been content with things like big screen 4K TV's or even their handheld devices for watching at home or on the go, the latest attempt to leap forward from these is just around the corner, in the form of Meta's VR Glasses. It's important to note that these are not the latest version of the smart glasses that have existed on the market since 2021, as they're explicitly not designed to be used while engaged in other activity. Instead, they're a cutting edge virtual/augmented reality system intended to bring together multiple work and entertainment options while idle.

I recently had the opportunity to try these glasses for myself, and their potential, especially for home viewing, is amazing. That said, there are some restrictions to them which, unless changed, mean they won't be replacing our existing personal devices anytime soon.

Although virtual reality, or VR, has existed in some form for decades, it's mostly been utilized as a gimmick more than a viable first choice for media. Fortunately, the folks behind Meta VR Glasses seem to understand this. I got to see a clip from the recent concert doc "Billie Eilish — Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour (Live in 3D)" on the glasses, and the experience was like I was watching it on a movie theater screen. That is to say that the aspect ratio was exactly the same as its theatrical exhibition, and the 3D display was pitch perfect. Turning my head in any direction didn't move the "screen," but kept it fixed in front of me, as if it was a physical object in the space, which is a very smart design.

While the James Cameron documentary acted as a demo of how watching most films and shows on the glasses would go, the Meta employees next showed me what they're calling "Enhanced Cinema." Using a clip from "Avengers: Infinity War" in which Thor (Chris Hemsworth) constructs Stormbreaker, the presentation was almost exactly akin to the Cosm experience. This meant that the film was playing on a similar fixed "display" in front of me, while all around me (literally 360 degrees — I checked!) was the environment of the forge on Nidavellir. It's an effect that's totally immersive but not distracting, nor does it betray the original intent of the film itself. After being told that Meta has an exclusive license with the IMAX corporation to present movies filmed for that format on the glasses, I have no doubt that the device could brilliantly replicate those screens for home viewing, and that's incredibly exciting.

While the Meta VR Glasses are not intended to replace a smartphone or similar device, they do seem to do a lot of what those devices do, only bigger and better. From working on VR video games and multiple computer monitors at once to allowing you to watch sports games as they broadcast while seeing the view from courtside, the glasses seem almost too good to be true as a personal media device.

This is where the catches come in. For one thing, watching something with other people at the same time can only occur depending on the content. For another, though they're engineered to be used while stationary, the temptation for people to wear them in public while walking (or, god forbid, driving) exists, and it's quite troubling. Then there's the fact that the glasses seem designed to only work with whatever services and content Meta allows. This means that us physical media fans are SOL, and as with any all-digital service, the content available on the glasses could be subject to change (or disappear) at any time. That's a lot to ask for a device priced at $1,299.99 USD, which is about the same as a new iPhone.

Note: Following publication, a representative for Meta did inform us that the VR glasses will support playback devices that are compatible via a wired DisplayPort-over-USB-C connection, meaning that additional content (like physical media) that the consumer has control over may be viewable on the glasses.

Right now, Meta's killer app beyond the tech itself are its exclusive licenses, such as with IMAX and James Cameron's Lightstorm Entertainment. The only way it'll compete with devices already on the market is if it can consistently deliver the quality experiences I got to have with it while being as user friendly as possible. If the glasses prove they can be used at home and on the go as smoothly as an iPhone can now, then they could be a game changer. Until then, they're just a gimmick, albeit a really nice one.

#3458. 2026's Most Viral Movie with 97 Rotten Tomatoes Score Sets Streaming Date

You are not ready for what Nathan Fielder has in store

In recent years, Nathan Fielder has rightfully earned a place as one of the most provocative figures in modern comedy. Most recently, the actor, filmmaker, and pilot (it’s a long story) co-directed You Can See Everything, a three-hour, brain-bending documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in the days before Holmes began her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

Despite this seemingly obscure premise, the A24 movie has exceeded all expectations, grossing an impressive $93 million on a $7 million budget to become the 10th highest-grossing documentary of all time. The film has received widespread critical acclaim, with a 97% Tomatometer score and an even more impressive 97 average review score on Metacritic. Audiences are equally enthusiastic; the movie has a 95% user score on Rotten Tomatoes.

According to WhenToStream’s sources, You Can See Everything is coming to Video On Demand (VOD) and digital platforms on Nov. 24, 2026. This would put the movie on streaming right before Thanksgiving; one can hope it leads to many awkward Turkey Day meals. While we don’t know how much the movie will cost to rent or buy, it will likely be priced between $19.99 and $24.99 to rent, as has become standard for early digital releases. You Can See Everything is still in theaters in the U.S. and hasn’t opened worldwide yet. It’s coming to the U.K. on Nov. 20, and to France on Dec. 30.

It’s difficult to explain what makes You Can See Everything so mesmerizing without spoiling its bizarre twists and turns, but the gist is that the movie pitches itself as one thing, before slowly spiraling into something else. Fielder once again shows his ability to squeeze the absurdity out of people and situations, as he did on Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, leading to increasingly ridiculous, self-referential circumstances built around deception and performance.

The movie intersects with many contemporary issues, including the increasing right-wing radicalization of tech bros, and grows increasingly meta until it eventually calls into question whether documentaries can really uncover the “truth” at all. There’s a lot going on, and it’s best to see the madness unfold yourself.

#3457. New Scientific Analysis Suggests Jeffrey Epstein Was Murdered. His Brother, For One, Feels Validated.

One day in August 2019, Mark Epstein was having breakfast at a Virginia hotel when he looked at the TV and saw CNN reporting that his older brother, Jeffrey Epstein, had died by suicide in a Manhattan federal prison. As jarring as the report was, he had no reason to doubt it.

“I knew he wouldn’t want to live the rest of his life in jail,” Mark told Vanity Fair this week. “He had no children to worry about. Our parents were gone. He knew he didn’t have to worry about me.”

Mark says he finished his omelet and headed back to New York. Then, like so many other Americans, he started to become skeptical of the official narrative.

Over the last seven years, the endless conspiracy theories surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death have largely been relegated to the backwaters of YouTube and Reddit, while local and federal authorities have stuck to the suicide story. But this week there was a breakthrough. On Monday, Michael Freeman, a leading forensic scientist who testified for the prosecution in the trial of Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd, issued the most legitimate challenge to date to the prevailing consensus.

Freeman presented his findings at a historic London legal society, saying, “The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging.” In a New York Times story published the same day as the presentation, Freeman told the publication that he had no view on who might have killed Jeffrey: “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” Along with several global news outlets, including CBS and the BBC, the paper covered the presentation with a straight face even as it noted that Freeman’s efforts to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal had thus far been rejected.

The relationship between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein has loomed large over the president’s second term.

In his thick Brooklyn accent, Mark Epstein, who has long been trying to prove that his brother was murdered while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges, excitedly recounted this new development over the phone the day after Freeman’s presentation, which he attended.

“This crosses all party lines,” Mark said. “Most people believe he didn’t commit suicide. So it’s a mystery. People want an answer to that. I think now they have the answer.”

Mark emphasized that the story of the recent findings was not about him but rather about his brother’s death and Freeman’s work. It was Freeman who reached out to him, Mark said, based on what the scientist independently thought was shoddy work on Jeffrey’s autopsy, and Mark agreed to turn over all the records, reports, and photographs he had as next of kin.

“I want to make it really clear,” he said. “I didn’t pay for this. He’s never asked me for anything other than the information, which I gave him willingly. And he’s been studying this. As a matter of fact, the night before last was the first time I ever met him face-to-face.”

Still, Mark has made his suspicions both his calling card and his personal mission in recent years. After working in real estate investing and serving as the chair of Cooper Union’s board of trustees, he had his own business dealings come under some scrutiny as Jeffrey’s life and crimes dominated political and cultural discourse beginning in the late 2010s—Jeffrey allegedly housed models and employees in an Upper East Side building that was predominantly owned by his brother’s real estate holding company. In the years since his brother’s death, Mark has said that Jeffrey “definitely had dirt” on Donald Trump, and he became a minor fixation amid the Epstein files rollout on account of emails containing banter between him and his brother. (Trump has denied any prior knowledge of Jeffrey’s crimes and said that the release of the Epstein files “totally exonerated” him.) Mark has dismissed a suicide note purportedly written by Jeffrey as a fabrication.

Jeffrey’s death certificate initially said “pending further study” in regard to the cause of death, rather than ruling it a homicide or suicide, but the chief medical examiner ruled it a suicide days later. “All the pathologists I’ve spoken to,” says Mark, “they said, [if] an initial death certificate says ‘pending further study,’ you don’t get an answer usually for weeks or more because something’s being studied.” Mark hired the celebrity forensic pathologist Michael Baden to observe and evaluate the autopsy, and Baden previously stated that “the evidence points to homicide.” Federal officials’ handling of the matter in the years to come only amplified Mark’s concern.

“You know a suicide when you see one,” FBI director Kash Patel said last year while he was under fire for not producing any proof of the Epstein conspiracies he had been touting during his time as a mere conservative podcast personality, “and that’s what that was.”

“I actually laughed out loud when I heard that,” Mark said, “because I thought, How many suicides has this fucking jackass actually seen?”

So who does Mark think killed his brother?

“It’s like in a Mob hit,” he said. “You try to find who the hit man was, and then you try to find who ordered the hit.” The hit man, he figured, could only be someone among a limited number of people: prison employees and other prisoners who had been on Jeffrey’s security tier. “Then the question becomes,” said Mark, “who would have the ability to orchestrate this in a federal prison, and who would have the ability to have the DOJ cover it up?” He couldn’t think of anyone besides Trump. (Trump has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection to Jeffrey’s death; in a 2023 interview with Tucker Carlson, when asked whether Jeffrey could have been killed, he said, “Oh sure, it’s possible. I mean, I don’t really believe—I think he probably committed suicide.”)

I thought Mark and I had developed some rapport over the conversation, particularly after I mentioned that I’d attended the same Coney Island middle school where he and his brother had been students; I emphasized that I was trying to listen to him carefully and take him seriously. But there was a bit more rancor in his tone after I said it was still difficult to believe that the Department of Justice could have successfully covered up the murder of the most high-profile prisoner in the world.

“If you don’t think that after what I just told you,” Mark said, “then you, sir, are a fucking idiot also.”

#3456. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3455. 10 Years Ago Today: The Harry Potter Universe Expanded With A Star-Studded Spin-Off

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Harry Potter" is perhaps the defining franchise of the 2000s, but all good things must come to an end. That end originally came in 2011 with "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2" which had the biggest opening ever up to that point in cinema history. But creator J.K. Rowling and Warner Bros. weren't content to let the Wizarding World end there. Ten years ago, they expanded the universe with a star-studded spin-off.

Set decades before Harry Potter was even born, 2016's "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them," which opened 10 years ago today, brought the action to America and focused on entirely new characters within the Wizarding World. Specifically Newt Scamander, played by Oscar-winner Eddie Redmayne. Redmayne had an unexpected inspiration for his performance, namely film icon Buster Keaton. The movie itself was loosely based on an in-universe textbook mentioned in the main series, with Rowling eventually releasing a version of the book, though it didn't contain a narrative.

The resulting prequel/spin-off takes place in 1926 centered on magizoologist Newt Scamander as he arrives in New York during a worldwide tour to research and rescue magical creatures. A mysterious magical being begins causing chaos in NYC, which threatens to expose the wizarding world to the muggles of Earth.

Redmayne was far from the only big star to secure a role in the spin-off. The stacked cast also includes but is not limited to Katherine Waterston, Dan Fogler, Alison Sudol, Samantha Morton, Ezra Miller, and Colin Farrell. "Fantastic Beats" also cast Johnny Depp as Grindelwald in a surprise appearance. Arguably the most important casting decision the movie made, with the benefit of hindsight.

J.K. Rowling wrote the script for "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" personally, which wasn't the case with the other "Harry Potter" movies. David Yates, who helmed the final four "Harry Potter" movies, was recruited to tackle the spin-off as well, providing a sturdy hand.

The majority of the core cast were on the upswing. This movie was expected to be a big break for all of them. In many ways, it was. "Fantastic Beasts" was dubbed a worthy extension of the Wizarding World in many reviews, with audiences tending to agree. Even if it wasn't effusive praise, it was good enough.

The movie was released in November 2016 and did quite well for itself, pulling in $816 million at the global box office. That was more than enough to convince Warner Bros. to double down, with four "Fantastic Beasts" sequels announced before the first one even hit theaters. Everyone involved fully expected this to be the long-term future for the "Harry Potter" franchise. What's perhaps most surprising about that, especially in light of the first movie's success, is the fact that the words Harry Potter don't appear anywhere in the title. All the same, audiences found it.

The train had left the station and everyone involved had every reason to believe, on paper, that people would show up for the sequels en masse. After all, the first installment scored well enough with critics and was the eighth-biggest movie of 2016 overall. Unfortunately, the future had different plans.

Warner Bros. and director David Yates wasted no time, with the second "Fantastic Beasts" installment dated for November 2018. Much of the cast returned, with new additions entering the fold. But in no small part due to forces beyond the studio's control, "The Crimes of Grindelwald" doomed "Fantastic Beasts."

The sequel pulled in more than $650 million at the box office, but made a lot less domestically and had to rely on international audiences to bail it out. Then there's the Depp of it all. Controversy started swirling around the actor due to his public feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard, involving accusations of domestic abuse. Depp later dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise following a court case verdict. Mads Mikkelsen took over as Grindelwald in "The Secrets of Dumbledore," but the writing was on the wall.

The third installment made hardly more than $400 million globally, failing to break even theatrically. "The Secrets of Dumbledore" proved that the magic was gone, despite the appeal of Jude Law as a younger Albus Dumbledore in a lead role. The cast continued to be star-studded all along the way but, at a certain point, appealing casts only go so far. Especially in the 2020s when audiences are more content than ever to stay at home and stream something from the couch.

Controversy and middling results with diminishing returns eventually derailed "Fantastic Beasts." Ten years ago though, the spin-off arrived with a great deal of promise and a lot of potential. That potential just never proved out.

You can grab "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

There are some shows on the 2026 TV schedule where I never need to worry if my favorite characters are going to die. That’s very much not the case with Yellowjackets’ impending final season. Tons of key people on the show have already kicked the bucket, and I don’t expect things to slow down before we say goodbye to the series forever. But what do the minds behind the series think about committing make-believe murder on the series so far?

As Yellowjackets fans, we’ve endured everything from Jackie Taylor freezing to death in the Season 1 finale to Van Palmer’s shocking stabbing last season. I asked the show’s creators, Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson, about the hardest death to write so far, and Lyle pointed out one big one she’s not over yet. Here’s what she told CinemaBlend:

One that was really difficult was filming Coach Scott's death. We've had a longstanding friendship and working relationship with Stephen Krueger, and we absolutely love him. And so, it was hard. It was really difficult to say goodbye to that character. But they're all difficult. Every single one of them.

Oof, yeah… Coach’s death was a rough one. Last season, we learned the details of Scott’s demise after the Yellowjackets’ cabin was burned to the ground. Then, he was put on trial by the Yellowjackets, and Shauna ordered Melissa to incapacitate him, which she did by slashing his Achilles tendon. After that, he’s left in agonizing pain and decides to stop eating and essentially begs Natalie to kill him.

Honestly, I totally agree with Lyle here. This was the most difficult death to watch, especially since we saw Coach decline over a number of episodes and felt his impending death coming. I love Yellowjackets, but I have to admit this was a really rough chapter in the series to sit through. While Lyle had to call out Coach’s death, my question wasn’t an easy one to answer. In her words:

They’re all really hard. I mean, because you spend so much time with these characters, and it sounds like such a corny cliché, but like they do kind of start to feel like your children. Like you created them.

On the flip side of things, they’ve already reached the finish line of the series. All that’s left is for us to watch it. Nickerson said it did get easier to kill characters off in the final season, saying this:

The longer you go in the show, I feel like the character is always hard to kill, but at least on a human level, it gets easier because, you know, the show will end eventually. So it's like, again, everybody's gonna need new jobs eventually, right?

Uhh… What does this mean? Who’s going to be safe and who’s going to die? I have no idea (and even the cast was left in the dark about spoilers), but I know I trust the writers to shock, surprise and make me feel a lot of things.

The premiere of Yellowjackets Season 4 airs on Friday, November 20 on SHOWTIME and with a Paramount+ subscription. I’m so curious who will be left standing by the end, and what Melanie Lynskey means by the series getting “crazier” and having a “fun ending”.
