#3453. Lux Pascal, Sarah Pidgeon, Ella Rubin, and More Glammed Up for Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry Dinner

“That is the highest compliment you could give anyone!” Lux Pascal says after I tell her she looks like Megan Draper from Mad Men. We’re at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner, held at Daniel Humm’s new eponymous restaurant, Humm, in the West Village. Pascal is in a ’60s black modish leather minidress that she’s paired with a cat eye. On her wrists are Chanel’s Première Galon watch and Coco Crush bracelets, which, like her rings and earrings, are all dotted with diamonds. As I look around, most of the celebrities dressed by the brand are wearing looks that show off their French fine accessories. Ella Rubin, the Gen Z star of the hit teen TV show Sterling Point, has upgraded a simple pair of vintage Levi’s with a sleek black-and-gold Première Ribbon watch and several diamond rings. This is not a night for hidden gems.

The Pierre Yovanovitch–designed restaurant is a verified New York power room at the moment: There’s Derek Blasberg talking to Sarah Pidgeon about books—War and Peace gets a name-check—and Architectural Digest’s Amy Astley in a corner with Metropolitan Museum of Art board member Robert Denning. Indrė Rockefeller is here, as is stylist Vanessa Traina. In a feat of fun seating arrangements, the Chanel team has sat Rubin next to another young Ella: Beatty, the recent star of Monster and daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening. (Although, with all due respect to those lovely Ellas, the two neighbors I’d most like to eavesdrop on are Devon Lee Carlson and Jack Harlow.) At the bar I hear two fashion people gossiping about industry hiring rumors: “Lauren Sherman says there’s two people in the running,” they whisper about some gig. I think I know what they’re talking about, but not enough to print it.

Laura Love and Devon Lee Carlson on November 17, 2026, in New York City (Photo by Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage)

Guests mill about because there’s much to mill about: Humm’s filled his restaurant with dozens of notable, site-specific artworks. Louise Bourgeois supplied 24 watercolor paintings, as well as a fantastical sterling silver cast of one of her sculptures, situated by the bar. (Tonight it’s serving mezcal sours with guava and an apple brandy highball.) Francesco Clemente painted not one, not two, but four celestial murals across two months, with motifs of abstract stars, animals, trains, and clocks. On the walls in the main dining room are 12 pigment drawings by Roni Horn. Then there’s all the work by Rashid Johnson: In the lounge—which for this event doubles as a red carpet—hangs his painting Untitled Homes. With Yovanovitch, he also built a custom host stand cast in aluminum and painted red. It’s so textural that you can see the fingerprints, and a number of guests gather around it as the maître d’ explains Johnson’s artistic process like he’s a docent at The Met.

Chanel has decorated the tables with long taper candles and arrangements of deep fuchsia peonies and burgundy garden roses. Waiters serve Humm’s signature everything caviar bagels. When I think about ordering something other than the chicken, a waiter tells me not to. He’s right.

At the end of the night, after most guests are a few glasses of red wine (or martinis) deep, Pidgeon herself grabs a microphone. The event, as it turns out, has a surprise performer: girlsweetvoiced. “She captures something that’s very honest,” Pidgeon says of the emerging singer-songwriter, who then belts out a cover of Joni Mitchell’s “California.” Title aside, it’s been a very New York night.

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3451. PlayStation Network Outage Hits On GTA 6 Release Day Eve

PS5 users are reporting widespread technical issues as GTA 6 rolls out

What happens when a potential 250 million people try logging into a server at the same time? Problems, that's what. Thursday, Nov. 19 is the official release day for Grand Theft Auto 6 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, and it appears Sony's platform, commonly known as PlayStation Network, is already buckling the day before under enormous demand for the world's most hyped game.

Many PS5 users tried to plan ahead by preloading the game starting on Nov. 10. Sony surely anticipated potential issues — the company has publicly treated GTA 6's release as if it were a first-party game — but that did little to prevent outages. Players around the world are facing messages like "Sony services are busy," "Too many failed connection attempts," or a mishmash of different errors. Though Sony's official status tracker currently lists the network as healthy, websites like Down Detector are seeing a sudden jump in reports related to the service. Most PS5 players say they're experiencing login issues with the PlayStation network, but there are also many reports of PSN server connection issues and update and download hiccups.

Whether you've seen codes like WS-116449-5, CE-34861-2, or WS-37505-0, they all point to the same thing: PlayStation's servers are facing serious strain.

GTA 6 is the follow-up to one of the most successful video games of all time, so the number of people trying to log in at once and download the game is likely massive. In the United States, it's the early afternoon — so many GTA fans probably just got off work and are all trying to do the same thing.

Though GTA 6 is not a multiplayer game that requires an online connection, players must download the title and its mandatory updates before they can enjoy it. This would have been the case even if GTA 6 had been printed on a disc — seemingly all major games require a day-one download for new patches or security reasons, like the recent PS5 jailbreak situation. This means that millions of people are trying to download hundreds of gigabytes of data at the same time, which was never going to end well.

There's no timeline for when PlayStation's servers might stabilize — and by extension, GTA 6 — but given the importance of this release, Sony are undoubtedly working on it.

Grand Theft Auto 6 officially launches on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

#3450. Avengers: Doomsday's PG-13 Rating Explained

We are a month away from potentially the biggest box office weekend of 2026, with Dunesday set to blow Barbenheimer out of the water as both "Dune: Part Three" and "Avengers: Doomsday" make their way into theaters. These movies are aimed at similar audiences, yet they're vastly different when it comes to their tones and approaches to adapting popular characters for the big screen. Indeed, where Denis Villeneuve's cinematic takes on the "Dune" books have so far been somber and introspective, the road to "Doomsday" has been paved almost entirely with nostalgia.

To be sure, between Robert Downey Jr. returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (this time to play Doctor Doom), the latest Avengers roster featuring multiple beloved characters from the MCU's past, and several actors reprising their roles from 20th Century Fox's "X-Men" films, "Doomsday" has had no problem catching the attention and interest of virtually every kind of moviegoer out there. After all, where "Dune: Part Three" can afford to target older audiences given the mature themes of its source material, "Doomsday" is aimed at everyone with a pulse and a heartbeat.

Hence, it's no surprise to learn that the new "Avengers" movie is now officially rated PG-13, just like almost every other previous film entry in the MCU since 2008 (save for "Deadpool & Wolverine"). Per FilmRatings.com, the film earned this rating from the Motion Picture Association (MPA) based on its "violence/action, bloody images, and language."

Just in case it needs to be said, "Avengers: Doomsday" was never going to be rated anything other than PG-13. The MCU's movies, in general, tend to feature too much intense action for any of them to garner a mere PG rating, yet they also tend to avoid going overboard into full-blown adult territory. At the same time, the explanation for its rating suggests "Doomsday" will make good on its promise of being one of the darker installments in the franchise.

Keeping that in mind, Marvel Studios and Disney were never going to allow a movie as costly as this one to get slapped with an R rating either, lest it severely limit the number of people who can pay to see it in a theater. And yes, "Deadpool & Wolverine" managed to become a massive success with an R-rating, but that was a different situation. Since the first two "Deadpool" films had been R-rated, it might've actually hurt the movie financially if it had tried to take the larger "Deadpool" property in a more family-friendly direction.

That's not to suggest that "Doomsday" won't be sufficiently dark or violent, though. Just too long ago, in fact, Sam Raimi pushed the PG-13 rating as far as humanly possible with 2022's "Doctor Strange In the Multiverse of Madness," the most gruesome Marvel movie yet. As you may recall, that film was filled with incredibly brutal death scenes, legitimate jump scares, and upsetting imagery that's not suitable for younger audiences. On the other hand, we can probably safely assume "Doomsday" won't push the envelope that far, given everything that's riding on it.

You can see what "Avengers: Doomsday" has to offer for yourself when it opens in theaters on December 18, 2026.

I don’t know about you, but my curiosity about Robert Downey Jr. in Avengers: Doomsday just keeps growing. Now, with just a month between us and Doomsday, RDJ got real about where he was at with the MCU before he got the call to join it again.

Downey was revealed to be Doomsday’s Victor von Doom in the summer of 2024, during Marvel’s Hall H panel at San Diego Comic-Con. It was a huge surprise not only to fans but to the actor, too. As the Oscar winner shared:

#3447. Avengers: The Kang Dynasty's Scrapped Doctor Doom Twist Explained By Marvel's Kevin Feige

As we march ever closer to "Avengers: Doomsday," it's easy to forget this movie was supposed to look very different. The original lead-in to "Avengers: Secret Wars" was supposed to be "Avengers: The Kang Dynasty," as directed by Destin Daniel Cretton (who had already helmed "Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings" for Marvel and would go on to direct "Spider-Man: Brand New Day").

Kang the Conqueror (Jonathan Majors), a time traveler who hails from the 31st century, appeared as the main villain of "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." A post-credits scene debuted the "Council of Kangs," or all of Kang's variants from a multiverse full of different timelines. But "Quantumania" earned unenthusiastic reviews upon its release in February 2023, and worse, Majors was arrested for assault the following month. (He was found guilty, and then fired by Marvel/Disney, in December 2023.)

Yeah, not exactly the launching pad you want for your next Thanos. Cue a pivot, and the announcement at San Diego Comic-Con 2024 that "Kang Dynasty" had been reworked into "Avengers: Doomsday," featuring Robert Downey Jr. returning to Marvel but as Doctor Doom, not Iron Man, as well as the return of "Infinity War" and "Endgame" directors Joe and Anthony Russo.

Now, this all seems like a "break glass in case of emergency" situation. But Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige, sitting down with Empire Magazine, now claims that even before "The Kang Dynasty" became "Doomsday," Kang was planned to be a red herring for Doom:

"People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan's issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that. [...] It probably would still have been called 'The Kang Dynasty,' but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie."

Kevin Feige, noting the "very delicate" situation with Jonathan Majors, told Empire that "[Marvel] didn't want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment." He acknowledged the changes to "The Kang Dynasty" started after the bad reception and underperformance of "Quantumania," noting:

"'Quantumania' was not received the way we would have liked. There are many elements of that that we're proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [The Kang Dynasty] even at that point."

Reading between the lines of Feige's claims, it would appear that once Majors was fired, the studio decided to push forward with Doom as the villain from the start instead of recasting Kang. But is this credible? I'll admit my first thought while reading this was, "Yeah, right!"

In his Empire interview, Feige appears to say the plans to bring in Doom to supplant Kang happened after the release of "Quantumania" but before Majors' arrest. "Quantumania" was released on February 17, 2023, and Majors was arrested on March 25, 2023. That seems like a pretty slim window to rework "The Kang Dynasty."

In November 2023, Variety reported that — at the annual Marvel Studios retreat held that past September — studio leadership was actively discussing how to move forward with Kang. ("Marvel is truly f***ed with the whole Kang angle," an insider was quoted as saying.) Apparently, the Marvel brain trust discussed replacing Kang with another villain, Doom specifically being named, as well as bringing back Avengers who died in "Endgame," like Robert Downey Jr. as Iron Man, to gin up excitement. As we now know, that's basically what Marvel did.

During a November 2023 appearance on the "Hot Mic" podcast, journalist Jeff Sneider claimed that Doom would appear in the then-upcoming "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" (which he did) as set up for him to show up in "Avengers: Secret Wars." However, Sneider said in that same interview that, "It'd be inaccurate to say [Doom is] the villain."

But Doom is the villain of Marvel Comics overall. The only reason the Marvel Cinematic Universe waited so long to use him is because 20th Century Fox held the film rights to his character. Once the Disney and Fox merger was completed in 2019, and Doom became available to Marvel Studios, Doom had to be high on any list of characters being considered for inclusion.

The "Secret Wars" comics — both the 1984 original and the 2015 pseudo-remake — also feature Doom as the main villain. In both, he attains godlike power and rules over a domain called Battleworld. If you're adapting "Secret Wars," the thought of using Doom has to cross your mind.

Kevin Feige's claim that Doom would take over "midway" through "The Kang Dynasty" also aligns with supposed leaked plot summaries for "Doomsday," which assert that Doom initially presents himself as an ally before revealing his true intentions. If that's accurate, it appears the movie still has the broad structure of "The Kang Dynasty," just with no Kang.

On the other hand, "Secret Wars" (especially the 2015 one) is a culmination of Doom's character. Rushing right into him becoming a God Emperor of Battleworld, without him being the villain in a "Fantastic Four" movie first? Yeah, that sounds like something that was "accelerated," per Feige.

"Avengers: Doomsday" releases on December 18, 2026.

#3446. Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond—Revisit 007’s Style Legacy Here

There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

Pierce Brosnan, The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

As portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

When Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Daniel Craig as James Bond, Casino Royale, 2006.

Also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.

With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first new Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan, Die Another Day, 2002.

Roger Moore and Grace Jones, 1985, A View To a Kill, 1985.

Of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the company acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

Pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

Also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

In September, Pattinson was announced as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this new installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the big screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

The real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave new world of brand deals, anything is possible.

#3445. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

Spoilers for the first five episodes of Rings of Power Season 3 are ahead! You can stream the series with an Amazon Prime subscription.

On Rings of Power, we’ve spent seasons trying to figure out the identities of the wizards who were sent to Middle-earth. In Season 2, after we spent a lot of time guessing and theorizing, we learned that The Stranger was indeed Gandalf. However, the identity of the Dark Wizard was still unknown. In Season 3, his true name was finally revealed, though, and I asked the co-creator of the show why they wanted to make the Dark Wizard the Blue Wizard Pallando.

In Episode 3 of the season of Rings of Power that’s currently airing on the 2026 TV schedule, Gandalf has an interaction with the Secret Fire, where it’s revealed to him that five wizards were sent to save Middle-earth. That’s how we learned that Pallando, one of the two Blue Wizards, killed his partner, and it’s also when Gandalf learns that he’s been sent to save the corrupted Blue Wizard. When I asked co-creator Patrick McKay why they wanted to make the Dark Wizard Pallando, he began by saying:

Here's the thing that we do on the show: We trust our audience. We're really thinking of it as one 50-hour movie. That's always been the plan and the aspiration. That also means that when we introduce a new character, you might not know where his or her allegiances lie. You might not know his or her name, but we know, and we have a plan.

While the end of Rings of Power Season 2 made me think the Dark Wizard was Saruman (even though that actually makes no sense timeline-wise), the other prevailing theory was that he was a Blue Wizard. Now, it’s confirmed that that’s the case, and McKay told me they made this decision because of how fascinating the lore is behind these two rather mysterious characters:

And you know there is this great lore in Tolkien about the two blue wizards who went east. And Tolkien had different versions of it and different ideas he played with. And a recurrent theme was that maybe one of them went bad, and no one knows what happened to the other one. And then, you know, thinking about that and bringing our wizard, our hero wizard Gandalf, sounds good to say that now, into that story, now you're weaving, right?

At one point, Tolkien wrote that the Blue Wizards could have been “founders or beginners of secret cults and magic traditions that outlasted the fall of Sauron” (via ScreenRant). It’s not confirmed if this is used as inspiration for Rings of Power; however, it does point to the potential moral ambiguity surrounding these magical beings.

On the show, they ultimately decided to run with the notion that Pallando might have done something terrible and killed his partner. Exploring the complexities of that was very interesting to them, as McKay told me:

What might be interesting? Well, gosh, what if Pallando has murdered his partner, and that's where he got his power from, but maybe there's complexity to it. Maybe he has guilt over it. Maybe, you know, he even has a desire for redemption. But how much? And then building a story around that was one of the joys of this season. But you know, the idea of the Blue Wizards is always tantalizing to us as fans, and part of our job is the inner fanboy getting to play.

Well, now I’m certainly excited to see where things go from here. I want to see Gandalf and Pallando interact more. I want to know if Gandalf can help his fellow wizard get away from the evil. And I want to know more about why the Blue Wizard killed his friend.

Hopefully, that will be unveiled as Rings of Power wraps up its third season and releases Episodes 7 and 8 on November 25.

#3443. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3442. The Next Major Fantasy Franchise Has Been Brewing For Over 30 Years

Every new fantasy movie wants to be the next "Lord of the Rings," and every new fantasy TV series wants to be the next "Game of Thrones." But both mediums are littered with the corpses of projects that failed to capture the zeitgeist. That includes perfect little gems like "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves" (whose box office underperformance remains a crushing shame) and "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" (which has proven it's not easy to be "Game of Thrones" for a "Lord of the Rings" audience, even with a billion dollar budget).

Recently, you may have noticed a new fantasy franchise waiting in the wings. Well, "new" isn't the proper word, perhaps — millions of people are very familiar with it. But rather, new to the people who made "Lord of the Rings" and "Game of Thrones" a crossover success. I'm talking about Magic: The Gathering, the long-running fantasy card game that's been draining wallets and firing up imaginations since its debut in 1993, which is now poised to make the leap to the big and small screens with two different projects.

The first of them is a Netflix animated series called "Planeswalker" from showrunner Terry Matalas, who's already a geek favorite thanks to his strong work on "Star Trek: Picard" season 3 and Marvel's "VisionQuest." The second is a live-action feature film starring Maya Hawke from Legendary Pictures and Matt Johnson, the eclectic filmmaker behind titles as divergent as "Blackberry" and "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie." It's the kind of two-pronged attack that suggests the timing is right for Magic, the biggest fish in its fantasy tabletop pond, to leap into the mainstream ocean.

Magic is about to have its crossover moment, and I think it has the goods to back it up.

Despite being an avid tabletop gamer and RPG player for over 20 years, I'm new to Magic, having only started playing and collecting this year to prepare for the new "Star Trek" set. However, the game got its hooks in me something fierce, and what was intended to be a brief dalliance has transformed into a new hobby/obsession/addiction.

I was initially drawn to the gameplay and its time-tested mechanics: simple to learn, hard to master, and infinitely flexible to match the style you find most entertaining. But the more time I spent in gaming shops, reading the flavor text at the bottom of a particularly dangerous card, noticing recurring characters across years of art, or chatting with people who have been collecting and playing for decades, I found myself increasingly interested in the world behind the game. Specifically, I was drawn to how the game's definition of fantasy was malleable, willing to blend traditional sword-and-sorcery with traditional folklore, gothic horror, science fiction, nautical adventure, and even zany swings like weird Westerns and multidimensional racing. If there's a creative itch to be scratched, the "planeswalkers" who anchor the narrative will surely expose a new world that will do the job nicely.

It's a universe where anything feels possible, starring varied and instantly recognizable heroes and villains who can travel between vastly different worlds as they journey on epic quests. It's a grand canvas with 33 years of history, characters, lore, and storytelling to build upon. There's more than enough for a movie series and TV show to draw on while still having enough to branch out indefinitely from there.

Following the formal announcement of "Planeswalker" at MagicCon, I asked the clerk at a local gaming shop if he was invested in Magic: The Gathering's world or if he just liked playing the game. He was emphatic: the gameplay hooked him, but the world and the characters and the expansive narrative is what kept him coming back. He spoke of the characters and their world with a reverence I've seen others bring to "Star Wars" and similarly rich universes.

The thin line separating the corners of various fantasy fandoms has eroded. The countless fans who line up for Sarah J. Maas novels and the nerds who crack open Magic booster packs aren't quite a circle, but it's a Venn diagram with a lot of overlap. The kind of weirdo fantasy that is Magic's bread and butter is now mainstream. The timing has never been better to open the door to the people devouring fantasy in other mediums and make it clear that the world of Magic: The Gathering is for them, too.

In recent years, Magic has (sometimes controversially) brought in outside franchises like Final Fantasy, Marvel, and yes, "Star Trek," to entice new players to play the game via their "Universe Beyond" label. I can attest firsthand that this works. But Magic is a great game and a rich world. The main draw for new fans shouldn't be just familiar IP on a Magic card. It should be the original world, fleshed out over three decades, itself. That's where a first-rate movie or show can do the heavy lifting.

The people who go to movie theaters every week and scroll the Netflix Top 10 every night may not realize that Magic offers a world as deep as Middle-earth or Westeros. The film and TV show must treat this universe itself as the main event, the reason to hit play or buy a ticket. A Magic: The Gathering series or movie will need more than just its players to be a true success ... and all of those new viewers pulled into a compelling fantasy epic become potential new players once they realize the game offers more of what they see on their screen.

If this film and this show are good (and they've certainly rounded up some promising talent), the Magic universe could be the next obsession for fantasy movie and TV fans. Even those who have never stepped into a gaming shop in their lives.

#3441. The 10 greatest games to never get a GOTY nomination

The Game Awards announced its 2026 nominations yesterday, though not without controversy. Grand Theft Auto 6 — a game that isn't even out yet — leads the pack with eight nominations, including Game of the Year. No indies managed to get a GOTY nomination this year, despite the release of acclaimed games like Mina the Hollower and Big Walk. Several blockbusters — including Polygon favorites like Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave and Pokémon Pokopia — were also snubbed for the night's biggest award.

While there's a lot to be said about 2026's Game Awards snubs, some of the greatest games of all time never received a GOTY nomination. While the games below may have been nominated (or won) in other Game Awards categories, they never got their fair shot at Game of the Year honors.

Where to play: PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Dark Souls 3 was a gorgeous, somber conclusion to FromSoftware's groundbreaking Dark Souls trilogy. By speeding up the pace of combat, Dark Souls 3 bridged Bloodborne and Elden Ring, streamlining an already iconic gameplay loop. To close out its trilogy, FromSoft proved it had complete mastery over the gameplay style it innovated years earlier.

Despite widespread acclaim, Dark Souls 3 was not nominated for Game of the Year in 2016, only getting a nod for Best RPG. Fans should take comfort in the fact that 2016 was an absolutely stacked year, though, with Overwatch, Doom, and Inside all competing for top honors. There's also the fact that very difficult games face an uphill battle in the GOTY race.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Outer Wilds is hard to categorize. At once an open-world explorer, an action adventure title, and a puzzle game, it dropped a traditional combat focus in favor of rewarding curiosity and knowledge. Couple that with a tightly written story, and you have one of the most immersive, combat-free gaming experiences of the decade.

Outer Wilds faced even stiffer competition than Dark Souls 3. 2019 was a competitive year, with Control, Death Stranding, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, The Outer Worlds, and the Resident Evil 2 remake fighting for top honors. Several other great games, like Disco Elysium, Fire Emblem: Three Houses, and Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order also failed to secure nominations. So, for an indie game — which tend to build popularity via word of mouth — Outer Wilds was always a deserving but unlikely nomination.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

NieR:Automata this relatively obscure spin-off of Square Enix's Drakengard series to mainstream audiences. Its intricate, existential story and seamless transitions between bullet-hell, hack-and-slash, and side-scrolling gameplay left a mark on millions of gamers worldwide.

Automata lost the nomination race to games like Breath of the Wild, Super Mario Odyssey, and Horizon Zero Dawn — games with enormous mainstream appeal. Though Automata was a breakout critical and commercial success for its franchise, it still came from a relatively niche series. What's more, the game's heavy philosophical themes and dozens of endings may have been a bit opaque for voters.

Ghost of Yotei, the highly anticipated follow-up to 2020 GOTY nominee Ghost of Tsushima, is about as cinematic as a game can get. With influence from filmmakers like Takashi Miike (13 Assassins) and Shinichiro Watanabe (Cowboy Bebop), Ghost of Yotei even has a game mode inspired by the work of Seven Samurai director Akira Kurosawa. And, it shows off its stunning graphics and cinematic influences without compromising on fluid, intense gameplay.

Ghost of Yotei earned seven Game Awards nominations in 2025, including Best Direction, Narrative, Audio Design, Action/Adventure Game, and more. So many people were confused about how a game that, apparently had some of the best direction, design, action gameplay and storytelling of the year could miss out on a GOTY nomination. Polygon's Oli Welsh even said "you could have grown it in a lab to win Game of the Year." Unfortunately, Ghost of Yotei paid a sequel tax — critics thought it didn't distinguish itself from Ghost of Tsushima quite enough.

Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze deserved better. It's an absolute masterclass in platformer design, with carefully themed levels and gimmicks that feel purposeful. Developers mastered a sense of momentum, getting players to chain satisfying rolls, jumps, and precise landings. Also, everything is set to an absolutely classic soundtrack by composer David Wise.

Tropical Freeze came out in 2014, the first year of the Game Awards, alongside titles like Bayonetta 2, Dark Souls 2, and Dragon Age: Inquisition. So, it didn't quite fit in with the kind of vibe the early Game Awards honored. Also, Tropical Freeze was initially a Wii U game. While a Nintendo Switch port has brought the game to platformer fans nationwide, the commercial failures of the Wii U hindered its success.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Considered one of the best games of the 2010s, Hollow Knight dropped players into a vast, rich world with minimal guidance. Since 2017, millions of gamers have uncovered Hallownest's secrets, pieced together its tragic history, and died a lot. (It's a hard game!)

Hollow Knight didn't make a ton of headlines when it first came out. Like many other indie titles, it spread slowly via word of mouth. So, it lacked the kind of blockbuster momentum that can propel a game to a GOTY nod. Hollow Knight received an indirect nod last year through the nomination of its sequel Hollow Knight: Silksong, which lost out to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.

Where to play: PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Konami and Bloober Team's Silent Hill 2 revisits one of the greatest psychological horror games of all time. It faithfully recreated the suffocating atmosphere and emotional weight of the 2001 original, while upgrading its gameplay to modern survival horror standards. Stronger performances and updated graphics made the terror and tragedy of Silent Hill 2 accessible to a new generation of gamers.

But horror games can be a tough sell at The Game Awards. Though high-profile blockbusters like Resident Evil 2 have been nominated, the only horror-adjacent game to bring home GOTY was The Last of Us Part II in 2020. Silent Hill 2 was also a remake; remakes are rarely nominated and have never won GOTY.

Fire Emblem: Three Houses was the best-selling mainline Fire Emblem game of all time, catapulting the series into Nintendo flagship status. Its iconic route split drew players into an intricate tale of war, love, and betrayal. It also sparked years upon years of discourse and fan arguments, which continue to this day. That ought to count for something.

Like Outer Wilds, Three Houses faced stiff competition amid a stacked 2019 gaming lineup. Also, Three Houses was a bit rough around the edges, particularly graphically. Couple that with a monastery hub that can feel repetitive (and the fact that you need to play the game four times to get the full story), and it's easy to understand why Three Houses failed to secure a GOTY nomination. That doesn't make it hurt less, though.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Yakuza 0 took on a lot. It features two protagonists, a high-stakes crime drama, over-the-top combat, and a quirky sense of humor, all without losing the series' integral "cool factor." It succeeded with flying colors, telling an emotional story about two iconic characters while leaving room for an all-important disco mini game.

When it was released overseas in 2016, Yakuza 0 was hampered by what Parasite director Bong Joon Ho called "the one-inch tall barrier of subtitles." Without an English dub upon release (it would eventually get one via its 2025 Director's Cut release), Yakuza 0's viral popularity was a slow burn with Western audiences. Once it launched on Steam in 2018, Yakuza 0 nearly doubled its past sales, and is now the best-selling game in the series. It may be the game that inspired a thousand memes — and took the Yakuza series into the mainstream — but it wasn't an overnight blockbuster.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Of course, this list would not be complete without Mina the Hollower, one of the most baffling GOTY nomination snubs of this year. Its intricately designed levels took an insane amount of effort, rivaling any AAA game out right now. That effort resulted in one of the year's best games, a loving homage to early Zelda games, the Game Boy Color, and Gothic horror.

While it received a nod for best indie game, Mina the Hollower was left off an indie-free GOTY nomination list. Though it was, critically speaking, one of the best received games of the year, it looks as though The Game Awards voters focused on mainstream blockbusters this year. It's also very, very hard, which may have dulled its mass appeal.

What’s in pole position for gaming’s top prize? Let’s make some predictions

neir automata is pretty mid and wouldn’t have the love it has if it wasn’t for a gooner bait MC. the characters are more popular than the actual game is.

#3440. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Incest Storyline Is A Big Change From The Books – And It Could Have Been Much Worse

One does not simply walk into spoilers. This article discusses major plot details up to "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 6.

When it comes to a story as sprawling and complex as "The Lord of the Rings," not all adaptation changes are made equally. Throughout three seasons of "The Rings of Power," showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have given us plenty to choose from. Some, like the arrival of Gandalf (Daniel Weyman), make perfect sense — although technically he's not meant to be involved in the action until centuries later in the timeline, you can understand why the series' creatives would want to speed things up a bit. Others, like the decision to keep Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) apart for so long, took longer to come into focus.

While many of the headlines will center on the deception of Charlie Vickers' Sauron and his breakthrough in figuring out how to forge the One Ring, an under-the-radar twist revealed itself all the way in the west on the island kingdom of Númenor. For several episodes, we've watched rivals and royal cousins Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) come closer and closer to outright conflict over the throne. How they resolve this may seem to line up with author J.R.R. Tolkien's original telling, but the circumstances vary considerably.

Now we know why the Prime Video series changed things up. In the latest episode, their attempts to negotiate and avoid bloody civil war reach an impasse ... until Pharazôn finds an unexpected solution. Actually, make that a proposal. Yes, this is the moment "The Rings of Power" takes a page out of the "House of the Dragon" playbook. And it could've been much worse.

"The Lord of the Rings" may have a reputation as cozy, comforting fantasy with its plucky Hobbits and kindly old wizards, but don't look past the abject darkness at the heart of the story. J.R.R. Tolkien never shied away from the shortcomings of individuals throughout his tales — in fact, as a Catholic, he emphasized them. But all it takes is a cursory look at the lore and mythology preceding his most famous novels to realize just how much Middle-earth has in common with the likes of Westeros in "Game of Thrones."

Don't believe us? Look no further than how "The Rings of Power" begins to resolve one of its biggest storylines in Season 3. After several episodes of Númenor coming perilously close to tearing itself apart, we're left on an unsettling cliffhanger. The usurper Pharazôn suggests that he and Míriel repair this rift through an incestuous political marriage. It's clear from the look on Míriel's face that this is a measure of last resort, but everything about her arc thus far implies that she'll end up putting the greater good of the kingdom over her own desires (which, remember, are more romantically inclined towards Lloyd Owen's noble Elendil).

Still, this is far tamer than how Tolkien originally tells it. While the appendices found at the end of "The Return of the King" are light on details, other sources (like "The Silmarillion") explain how Pharazôn looked enviously upon the rightful heir Míriel, forced his cousin into marriage against her will and against all the laws of the land, and took power. Compared to this, "The Rings of Power" gives Míriel far more agency.

Those who know their J.R.R. Tolkien ought to be well familiar with where "The Rings of Power" is going next. (For those who don't, be advised this next section dives into major potential spoilers.) With only two episodes to go in Season 3 and the bulk of it likely taking place on the mainland, the Númenor plot will soon need to resolve itself. Míriel must still actually agree to Pharazôn's terms and avoid a costly battle, thus allowing their combined forces to look outwards and send their armada to assist the beleaguered Elves attempting to resist against Sauron.

But it's what comes next, almost certain to unfold in Season 4, that concerns us the most. With their power soon to be consolidated in an uneasy alliance, Míriel and Pharazôn will eventually have to contend with that pesky Dark Lord. According to the various texts, this is the pivotal inflection point that puts us on a path towards the inevitable Fall of Númenor. According to Tolkien's original writings, Númenor's entrance into the war has disastrous consequences. Granted, their fearsome army quickly overwhelms Sauron's own and leads to him being taken back to the island as a prisoner, but that's where all the troubles begin. Eventually, Sauron worms his way into Pharazôn's ear and convinces him to set his sights on the Valar themselves — a desperate gambit to stave off death among Mortal Men and seize the eternal life that's been denied them.

None of this ends well for Númenor, but we're getting ahead of ourselves. The final two episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 stream November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.

#3439. The 8 Greatest Cold War Books of All Time, Ranked

The second half of the 20th century was defined by the Cold War. The decades-long conflict shaped international politics, fueled devastating proxy conflicts, and brought humanity frighteningly close to annihilation. Unsurprisingly, these tensions provided fertile ground for novelists, particularly those interested in espionage.

The result was a deep and diverse body of work exploring the Cold War from every angle and perspective, covering many genres and introducing some of literature's most timeless settings, narratives, and characters. This list looks at some of the very best of them, from meticulously researched military thrillers to character studies about compromise and disillusionment.

"Why don't you pass the time by playing a little solitaire?" Many people will be familiar with the classic film, but The Manchurian Candidate actually started out as a novel. It focuses on Raymond Shaw, an American soldier who returns from the Korean War as a decorated hero after supposedly saving the lives of his fellow servicemen. However, the truth is considerably more disturbing. During his captivity, Raymond was subjected to an elaborate brainwashing experiment designed to transform him into an unwitting assassin.

Meanwhile, his former commanding officer, Bennett Marco, begins experiencing troubling nightmares that suggest their official recollections of the war are false. Building off that setup, the book becomes a chilling political thriller, as well as a striking time capsule for the paranoia and ideological hysteria of the 1950s. The cynicism and satire have aged surprisingly well.

"An alarm clock is a strange thing in a submarine." Shifting gears, we have Tom Clancy's breakout book, which turns Cold War tensions into a suspenseful, blockbuster entertainment. In The Hunt for Red October, Soviet commander Marko Ramius takes control of the Red October, an advanced nuclear submarine equipped with a revolutionary propulsion system that makes it exceptionally difficult to detect. When Ramius unexpectedly changes course toward the Atlantic, Soviet authorities launch a massive operation to intercept him.

Meanwhile, CIA analyst Jack Ryan becomes convinced that Ramius intends to defect to the United States, placing him at the center of a potentially catastrophic international confrontation. There is mystery and action aplenty here, but it's elevated by Clancy's meticulous research and attention to detail. He gets granular with the descriptions of submarine warfare, sonar systems, naval tactics, and the bureaucracy of intelligence operations.

"Sometimes the most important battles are fought without weapons." Winter of the World is the second entry in Ken Follett's sweeping Century Trilogy. It's a masterful historical epic that charts the major events of the 20th century through the eyes of a few families. The first book was all about the Great War and, here, the focus is on World War II and the early stages of the Cold War.

The sprawling cast includes characters from Britain, Germany, the Soviet Union, and the USA, whose personal ambitions and relationships become entangled with the major social forces of their time. Through them, the book brings many crucial historical moments to life, rendering them all in accessible prose and compelling plotting. As a result, a fairly weighty book winds up being quite a page-turner. Not for nothing, Winter of the World hit number one on the New York Times bestseller list.

"It was the beginning of his life." This is a gripping psychological thriller by Atonement's Ian McEwan. Set in Berlin during the 1950s, The Innocent centers on Leonard Marnham, a young British telecommunications technician recruited to assist with a secret Anglo-American intelligence operation. His assignment involves helping construct and maintain a tunnel beneath Soviet-controlled territory, allowing Western intelligence agencies to intercept sensitive communications.

However, Leonard's life changes dramatically when he begins a relationship with Maria Eckdorf, a German woman whose troubled past introduces complications far removed from his professional responsibilities. From here, we get an unusually smart and character-driven espionage story, expressed through McEwan's dependably brilliant prose. The Innocent gets pretty deep with its themes, too. Indeed, the title refers to the deluded belief that nations or individuals can engage in covert power struggles without getting blood on their hands.

"Some things are too important to be left to the intelligence services." This one is the opening entry in a trilogy (which itself is the first of three trilogies) about Bernard Samson, an MI6 officer who has spent much of his career operating in Berlin. Having grown up in the city, he understands the divided society intimately, as well as the complicated relationships between Western intelligence agencies and their Soviet counterparts.

His latest assignment involves extracting a valuable British agent from East Germany, but the operation becomes increasingly dangerous when evidence suggests that a Soviet mole has infiltrated British intelligence. Refreshingly, the book portrays spycraft as a grimy profession divided by personal rivalries and conflicting loyalties rather than glamorous adventures. Likewise, the protagonist is cynical and sarcastic, in stark contrast to the suave super-spies of classic espionage fiction.

"Innocence is like a dumb leper who has lost his bell, wandering the world, meaning no harm." This is one of the defining works by English novelist and journalist Graham Greene, who also wrote The Heart of the Matter and the novella that became the movie The Third Man. Set in Vietnam during the final years of French colonial rule, The Quiet American revolves around Thomas Fowler, a cynical British journalist who has become emotionally attached to the country despite his insistence on remaining politically neutral.

He then crosses paths with Alden Pyle, an idealistic young American whose enthusiasm for political theories contrasts sharply with Fowler's more experienced understanding of the conflict. Through these two men, the book examines the dangers of imposing ideological solutions on complex societies, especially as an outsider. It's something governments continue to fail to take to heart.

"The first one was a woman." One of the strongest James Bond books. The story begins with the Soviet counterintelligence organization SMERSH devising an elaborate operation to destroy 007. Their scheme involves Tatiana Romanova, a young cipher clerk who is instructed to pretend that she wishes to defect to the West. As an additional incentive, she offers to provide British intelligence with a valuable Soviet decoding machine. Bond is subsequently dispatched to Istanbul, though the true objectives of the operation are concealed from him.

Intriguingly, the entire first third of the novel doesn't feature Bond at all, instead detailing the inner workings of SMERSH in Moscow. All in all, From Russia with Love is a typically enjoyable mix of intrigue, espionage thrills, and juicy narrative switcheroos. Some of the series' most memorable supporting characters also appear here, particularly the resourceful Turkish operative Darko Kerim and the terrifying assassin Red Grant.

"What do you think spies are: priests, saints, and martyrs?" When it comes to quintessential Cold War books, it's hard to top The Spy Who Came in from the Cold, John le Carré's magnum opus. In it, we meet Alec Leamas, a disillusioned British agent whose network of agents in East Germany has been systematically dismantled. Following the death of his last remaining operative, Leamas is recalled to London, where his superiors devise an elaborate operation intended to undermine a powerful East German intelligence official.

To make the deception convincing, Leamas must appear to have become a bitter, alcoholic willing to betray his country. However, as the operation progresses, the line between calculated manipulation and genuine betrayal becomes increasingly blurred. The result is a hard-edged, world-weary spy story that captures the grimness of the Cold War in the 1960s, forever changing the genre in the process.

#3438. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3437. GTA 6 Officially Cuts A Controversial Franchise Feature After 25 Years

The mechanic has appeared in many GTA games, across multiple hardware generations

You can do anything you want in a Grand Theft Auto game, but the franchise has historically been defined by a handful of specific mechanics. Steal a car. Shoot pedestrians. And for better or worse, soliciting a prostitute. Grand Theft Auto 6, however, is an unusually realistic game that tells a humane story about a couple, and those shifts in approach are reflected in the game's actions.

Prostitutes made their debut as NPCs in 2001 with the release of Grand Theft Auto 3. These characters, which appeared on the game's streets at night, could be solicited by the player for $100. Though the encounters were explicit in nature, the animations at the time only showed the vehicle bouncing suggestively.

The arguably tame mechanic became infamous for two primary reasons. Many fans approach GTA as a chaos simulator, so players sometimes target sex workers indiscriminately. It became a running joke, for lack of a better word, for GTA fans to sleep with and immediately kill the women they hired. Once dead, the NPCs would drop the money the player used to hire them.

Another major source of the feature's infamy was Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas' Hot Coffee incident. In short, Rockstar designed a mini-game that allowed CJ, the protagonist, to have sex with a prostitute. Unlike GTA 3, this minigame didn't leave things to the imagination — the characters could be seen bent over and going at it. Rockstar pulled the minigame out of San Andreas for the official release, but the feature was still hidden in the game's files. In 2005, when San Andreas was ported to PC, modders found the minigame and released it to the public under the name Hot Coffee.

Many years later, after much legal rigmarole and multiple new games, Hot Coffee has defined the public's view of GTA as a franchise. Yet despite all the headaches Hot Coffee caused Rockstar, the developer nonetheless continued to include sex workers through Grand Theft Auto 5. In that game, the player purchase services by sex workers that were, in some cases, animated more scandalously than those in Hot Coffee. Rockstar's addition of a first-person view further heightened the intensity of these encounters. GTA V was also the first game to include a crass caricature of trans sex workers available for hire — a fact that was heavily decried by queer fans who felt Rockstar was punching down.

Now, 25 years after their original inclusion, hirable sex workers are not making a return in GTA 6. Given the game's enormous number of encounters, a sex worker could still appear somewhere in GTA 6. As a type of highly visible NPC, however, prostitutes are gone.

Rockstar did not immediately respond to a request for comment. However, a representative told Shacknews that “GTAVI is a game about a couple in a bind, lovers on the run. While we have taken a lot forward from previous GTA titles, everything we have implemented in VI has been done to support the spirit of the story we wanted to tell, and the gameplay systems we wanted to expand upon — things like wanted system, the radio, robberies and car theft."

The explanation makes sense given GTA 6's realism and heightened gore. Critics have already noted in their reviews that, for the first time ever, breaking the law or harming NPCs sometimes inspires guilt. Rockstar's justification has still disappointed fans who consider prostitutes a key pillar of the franchise. Most people don't seem to mind and appear content with being able to visit strip clubs.

"Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTAVI, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar's statement continued.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.
